entries.text: Blows given on the palm of the hand with a twisted handkerchief, instead of a ferula; a jocular punishment among seamen, who sometimes play at cards for wackets, the loser suffering as many strokes as he has lost games.
To pretend sickness.
To cast up one's accounts; to vomit.
You will ride a horse foaled by an acorn, i.e. the gallows, called also the Wooden and Three-legged Mare. You will be hanged.--See THREE-LEGGED MARE.
A military term for small beer, five pints of which, by an act of parliament, a landlord was formerly obliged to give to each soldier gratis.
A louse.
Water.
A pickpocket's associate, who receives the stolen goods, and runs off with them. CANT.
An inconsiderate foolish fellow.
A spoil-sport, a mar-all.
who carries his flag on the main-mast. A landlord or publican wearing a blue apron, as was formerly the custom among gentlemen of that vocation.
One who from drunkenness vomits into the lap of the person sitting opposite to him. SEA PHRASE.
Loose, turned adrift, discharged. SEA PHRASE.

(CAMBRIDGE), A certificate from the apothecary that you are INDISPOSED, (i. e.) to go to chapel. He sports an Aegrotat, he is sick, and unable to attend Chapel. or Hall. It does not follow, however, but that he can STRUM A PIECE, or sport a pair of oars.
Knights of the post, or false witnesses, said to attend Westminster Hall, and other courts of justice, ready to swear any thing for hire.
Unwilling. It went much against the grain with him, i.e. it was much against his inclination, or against his pluck.
Stuck fast, stopped, at a loss, ruined; like a boat or vessel aground.
A roasted turkey garnished with sausages; the latter are supposed to represent the gold chain worn by those magistrates.
A draught on the pump at Aldgate; a bad bill of exchange, drawn on persons who have no effects of the drawer.
An alehouse keeper.
A may-pole.
It is all holiday at Peckham, or it is all holiday with him; a saying signifying that it is all over with the business or person spoken of or alluded to.
He was beat all hollow, i.e. he had no chance of conquering: it was all hollow, or a hollow thing, it was a decided thing from the beginning. See HOLLOW.
A composition of all the different spirits sold in a dram-shop, collected in a vessel into which the drainings of the bottles and quartern pots are emptied.

The five alls is a country sign, representing five human figures, each having a motto under him. The first is a king in his regalia; his motto, I govern all: the second, a bishop in pontificals; motto, I pray for all: third, a lawyer in his gown; motto, I plead for all: fourth: a soldier in his regimentals, fully accoutred; motto, I fight for all: fifth, a poor countryman with his scythe and rake; motto, I pay for all.
The man is in his altitudes, i.e. he is drunk.
A lawyer who takes fees from both plaintiff and defendant, or that goes snacks with both parties in gaming.
A parish clerk.
He said Yes and Amen to every thing; he agreed to every thing.
Within ames ace; nearly, very near.
To fling dust or snuff in the eyes of the person intended to be robbed; also to invent some plausible tale, to delude shop-keepers and others, thereby to put them off their guard. CANT.
Bring your a-se to an anchor, i.e. sit down. To let go an anchor to the windward of the law; to keep within the letter of the law. SEA WIT.
Begging out of a prison window with a cap, or box, let down at the end of a long string.
A halter.
To manoeuvre the apostles, i.e. rob Peter to pay Paul; that is, to borrow money of one man to pay another.
(CAMBRIDGE.) Men who are plucked, refused their degree.

To talk like an apothecary; to use hard or gallipot words: from the assumed gravity and affectation of knowledge generally put on by the gentlemen of this profession, who are commonly as superficial in their learning as they are pedantic in their language.
A long bill.
Down with his apple-cart; knock or throw him down.

A bed made apple-pye fashion, like what is called a turnover apple-pye, where the sheets are so doubled as to prevent any one from getting at his length between them: a common trick played by frolicsome country lasses on their sweethearts, male relations, or visitors.
Pump water. APOTHECARIES LATIN.
A comical or eccentric fellow.
Hot. CANT.
A boat or wherry. Let us take an ark and winns, let us take a sculler. CANT.

Rogues who, in conjunction with watermen, robbed, and sometimes murdered, on the water, by picking a quarrel with the passengers in a boat, boarding it, plundering, stripping, and throwing them overboard, &c. A species of badger. CANT.
A bum fiddle.

To hang an arse; to hang back, to be afraid to advance. He would lend his a-e and sh-te through his ribs; a saying of any one who lends his money inconsiderately. He would lose his a-e if it was loose; said of a careless person. A-e about; turn round.
To fall arsy varsey, i.e. head over heels.

KING ARTHUR, A game used at sea, when near the line, or in a hot latitude. It is performed thus: A man who is to represent king Arthur, ridiculously dressed, having a large wig made out of oakum, or some old swabs, is seated on the side, or over a large vessel of water. Every person in his turn is to be ceremoniously introduced to him, and to pour a bucket of water over him, crying, hail, king Arthur! if during this ceremony the person introduced laughs or smiles (to which his majesty endeavours to excite him, by all sorts of ridiculous gesticulations), he changes place with, and then becomes, king Arthur, till relieved by some brother tar, who has as little command over his muscles as himself.
Breeches; coat, waistcoat, and articles.
A common reply to any question; still deemed wit at sea, and formerly at court, under the denomination of selling bargains. See BARGAIN.
Stealing brass weights off the counters of shops. CANT.
A church.
A parson. CANT.
Pickpockets who practice in churches; also churchwardens and overseers of the poor. CANT.
Acquainted with, knowing the business. Stow the books, the culls are awake; hide the cards, the fellows know what we intended to do.
Criminals in the stocks, or pillory.
Confused, unintelligible talk, such as was used at the building the tower of Babel.
One who slanders another behind his back, i.e. in his absence. His bosom friends are become his back biters, said of a lousy man.
Dead. He wishes to have the senior, or old square-toes, backed; he longs to have his father on six men's shoulders; that is, carrying to the grave.
He has saved his bacon; he has escaped. He has a good voice to beg bacon; a saying in ridicule of a bad voice.
Full-faced.
One of his majesty's bad bargains; a worthless soldier, a malingeror. See MALINGEROR.
A term used for one burned in the hand. He has got his badge, and piked; he was burned in the hand, and is at liberty. Cant.
Parish Pensioners. Cant.
A crew of desperate villains who robbed near rivers, into which they threw the bodies of those they murdered. Cant.
He gave them the bag, i.e. left them.
Fourteen; that number of rolls being allowed to the purchasers of a dozen.
Adulterated wine.
Money.
A jocular imposition, the same as a humbug. See HUMBUG.
To impose on any one by a falsity; also to jeer or make fun of any one.
To make a fool of any one, to humbug or impose on him.
Mine a-se on a bandbox; an answer to the offer of any thing inadequate to the purpose for which it is proffered, like offering a bandbox for a seat.
A bailiff or his follower; also a very fierce mastiff: likewise, a bandbox. CANT.

(WHIP.) Quite the thing, hellish fine. Well done. Compleat. Dashing. In a handsome stile. A bang up cove; a dashing fellow who spends his money freely. To bang up prime: to bring your horses up in a dashing or fine style: as the swell's rattler and prads are bang up prime; the gentleman sports an elegant carriage and fine horses.
To beat.
Great; a fine banging boy.
A nick name for a thresher, but applied to all the servants of a farmer.
A one-horse chaise, said to be so called by a Lord Chief Justice, from their being so frequently used on Sunday jaunts by extravagant shop-keepers and tradesmen.
A horse famous for playing tricks, the property of one Banks. It is mentioned in Sir Walter Raleigh's Hist. of the World, p. 178; also by Sir Kenelm Digby and Ben Jonson.
Rum, brandy, or any other spirits, that have been lowered with water.
A standing pole and two wash balls.
(CAMBRIDGE.) Barge-men on the river.

The shopman of a bow-wow shop, or dealer in second hand clothes, particularly about Monmouth-Street, who walks before his master's door, and deafens every passenger with his cries of--Clothes, coats, or gowns--what d'ye want, gemmen?--what d'ye buy? See BOW-WOW SHOP.
A parson's barn; never so full but there is still room, for more. Bit by a barn mouse, tipsey, probably from an allusion to barley.
An old dance to a quick movement. See Cotton, in his Virgil Travesti; where, speaking of Eolus he has these lines, Bounce cry the port-holes, out they fly, And make the world dance Barnaby.

A good job, or snack easily got: also shellfish growing at the bottoms of ships; a bird of the goose kind; an instrument like a pair of pincers, to fix on the noses of vicious horses whilst shoeing; a nick name for spectacles, and also for the gratuity given to grooms by the buyers and sellers of horses.
He died of the barrel fever; he killed himself by drinking.
A man under sentence of transportation; alluding to the convicts at Woolwich, who are principally employed in wheeling barrows full of brick or dirt.
A person dressed up in a tawdry manner, like the dolls or babies sold at Bartholomew fair.
To beat. I'll give him his bastings, I'll beat him heartily.
A beating.
Beating any one with a stick; from baton, a stick, formerly spelt baston.
We had a pretty batch of it last night; we had a hearty dose of liquor. Batch originally means the whole quantity of bread baked at one time in an oven.
An ox: beef being apt to batten or fatten those that eat it. The cove has hushed the battner; i.e. has killed the ox.
Bread and cheese and kisses.
A battle or bout at cudgels or fisty-cuffs, wherein more than two persons are engaged: perhaps from its resemblance, in that particular, to more serious engagements fought to settle royal disputes.
A term of ridicule applied to convicts, who sham illness, to avoid being sent to Botany Bay.
To ride bayard of ten toes, is to walk on foot. Bayard was a horse famous in old romances,

One who contracts to deliver a certain quantity of sum of stock in the public funds, on a future day, and at stated price; or, in other words, sells what he has not got, like the huntsman in the fable, who sold the bear's skin before the bear was killed. As the bear sells the stock he is not possessed of, so the bull purchases what he has not money to pay for; but in case of any alteration in the price agreed on, either party pays or receives the difference. Exchange Alley.
Rude, vulgar language, such as was used at the bear-gardens.
A travelling tutor.
I'll bring him to his bearings; I'll bring him to reason. Sea term.
To drink like a beast, i.e. only when thirsty.
Boots. Cant.
A slovenly fop; one finely dressed, but dirty.

A loose stone in a pavement, under which water lodges, and on being trod upon, squirts it up, to the great damage of white stockings; also a sharper neatly dressed, lying in wait for raw country squires, or ignorant fops.
A piece of sea wit, sported in hot weather. I am becalmed, the sail sticks to the mast; that is, my shirt sticks to my back. His prad is becalmed; his horse knocked up.
A beadle. See HERMANBECK.
I am for Bedfordshire, i.e. for going to bed.
Dressed out, over-dressed, or awkwardly ornamented.

A yeoman of the guards, instituted by Henry VII. Their office was to stand near the bouffet, or cupboard, thence called Bouffetiers, since corrupted to Beef Eaters. Others suppose they obtained this name from the size of their persons, and the easiness of their duty, as having scarce more to do than to eat the king's beef.
One having thick projecting eyebrows.
Dull, stupid.
A publican, or ale-house keeper.
Stones. The beggar's bullets began to fly, i.e. they began to throw stones.

He will dance at Beilby's ball, where the sheriff pays the music; he will be hanged. Who Mr. Beilby was, or why that ceremony was so called, remains with the quadrature of the circle, the discovery of the philosopher's stone, and divers other desiderata yet undiscovered.
All sorts of beer; that liquor being apt to cause eructation.
A red silk handkerchief, intermixed with yellow and a little black. The kiddey flashes his belcher; the young fellow wears a silk handkerchief round his neck.
The lungs.
The town crier.
Transportation for life: i.e. as long.
His eye was bigger than his belly; a saying of a person at a table, who takes more on his plate than he can eat.
An apron.
Food of all sorts.
A noisy bullying fellow.
The chief or leader of a mob; an idea taken from a flock of sheep, where the wether has a bell about his neck.
Good--BENAR. Better. Cant.
Good beer, or other strong liquor. Cant.
A good fellow. Cant.
Goodnight. Cant.
Counterfeiters of bills. Cant.
Counterfeiters of passes. Cant.
Worshipfully. Cant.
A fool. Cant.
Foolish.
A cant name for certain places in London, privileged against arrests, like the Mint in Southwark, Ben. Jonson. These privileges are abolished.

A small instrument used by house-breakers to force open doors. Bring bess and glym; bring the instrument to force the door, and the dark lantern. Small flasks, like those for Florence wine, are also called betties.
See BROWN BESS.
A wager.--TO BET. To lay a wager.
That's my eye, Betty Martin; an answer to any one that attempts to impose or humbug.
Surprised, confounded, out of one's senses; also bewrayed.
An afternoon's luncheon; also a fine hat; beaver's fur making the best hats,
Garnish money, or money for drink, demanded of any one having a new suit of clothes.
A boatswain's great axe. Sea term.
Supposed by the vulgar to be more binding than an oath taken on the Testament only, as being the bigger book, and generally containing both the Old and New Testament.
A sword. Bilboa in Spain was once famous for well-tempered blades: these are quoted by Falstaff, where he describes the manner in which he lay in the buck-basket. Bilboes, the stock; prison. Cant.
To go. Cant. Bing avast; get you gone. Binged avast in a darkmans; stole away in the night. Bing we to Rumeville: shall we go to London?
Brandy or other spirituous liquor. Cant.
A dram drinker. Cant.
A fine or affected word, which sailors jeeringly offer to chalk up on the binnacle.
Inconsiderate, thoughtless, easily imposed on.
Rogues of the same gang.

A term used among horse-dealers, for burning the mark into a horse's tooth, after he has lost it by age; by bishoping, a horse is made to appear younger than he is. It is a common saying of milk that is burnt too, that the bishop has set his foot in it. Formerly, when a bishop passed through a village, all the inhabitants ran out of their houses to solicit his blessing, even leaving their milk, &c. on the fire, to take its chance: which, went burnt to, was said to be bishoped. TO BISHOP the balls, a term used among printers, to water them.
Money. He grappled the cull's bit; he seized the man's money. A bit is also the smallest coin in Jamaica, equal to about sixpence sterling.
In writing. I have it in black and white; I have written evidence.
The art of picking a lock. Cant.
A copper or kettle. The pot calls the kettle black a-se. Cant.
He is down in the black book, i.e. has a stain in his character. A black book is keep in most regiments, wherein the names of all persons sentenced to punishment are recorded.
A lawyer. Cant.
We gave the bottle a black eye, i.e. drank it almost up. He cannot say black is the white of my eye; he cannot point out a blot in my character.
The greatest drawback on the farmer is the black fly, i.e. the parson who takes tithe of the harvest.

A shabby, mean fellow; a term said to be derived from a number of dirty, tattered roguish boys, who attended at the Horse Guards, and Parade in St. James's Park, to black the boots and shoes of the soldiers, or to do any other dirty offices. These, from their constant attendance about the time of guard mounting, were nick-named the black-guards.
A nick name given to the Recorder by the Thieves.
A jug to drink out of, made of jacked leather.
Newcastle upon Tyne, whose rich coal mines prove an Indies to the proprietors.
The first Monday after the school-boys holidays, or breaking up, when they are to go to school, and produce or repeat the tasks set them.
To rob chimney sweepers of their soot, bag and soot.
The Devil.
Bene Carlo wine; also port. A task of labour imposed on soldiers at Gibraltar, as a punishment for small offences.
To look blank; to appear disappointed or confounded.
To curse.
A calf. Cant.
Those cheated by Jack in a box. CANT.--See JACK IN A BOX.
A sheep. Cant.
Sheep stealing. Cant.
One who parts easily with his money, or bleeds freely.
A metaphor borrowed from fish, which will not bleed when stale.
A small quantity over and above the measure, usually given by hucksters dealing in peas, beans, and other vegetables.
Night, darkness.
Prisons, houses of correction, &c.
Finished. The game is blocked at both ends; the game is ended.
A riotous disorderly fellow.
A term used by tradesmen for bartering the different commodities in which they deal. Thus a hatter furnishing a hosier with a hat, and taking payment in stockings, is said to deal blood for blood.
The reward given by the legislature on the conviction of highwaymen, burglars, &c.
A jeering appellation for a soldier, alluding to his scarlet coat.
A favourite word used by the thieves in swearing, as bloody eyes, bloody rascal.

entries.word: TO BLOT THE SKRIP AND JAR IT
entries.text: To stand engaged or bound for any one. Cant.
He has bit the blow, i.e. he has stolen the goods. Cant.
A pipe. How the swell funks his blower and lushes red tape; what a smoke the gentleman makes with his pipe, and drinks brandy.
To confess, or impeach a confederate. Cant.
A discovery, or the confusion occasioned by one.
The mouth.--I have stopped the cull's blubber; I have stopped the fellow's mouth, meant either by gagging or murdering him.
To cry.
To look blue; to be confounded, terrified, or disappointed. Blue as a razor; perhaps, blue as azure.
Low spirits.
He has hoisted the blue flag; he has commenced publican, or taken a public house, an allusion to the blue aprons worn by publicans. See ADMIRAL OF THE BLUE.
Thieves who steal lead off houses and churches. Cant. To fly a blue pigeon; to steal lead off houses or churches.
A bullet.--Surfeited with a blue plumb; wounded with a bullet. A sortment of George R--'s blue plumbs; a volley of ball, shot from soldiers' firelocks.
Gin.
Gin. Blue ribband; gin.
Fierce, surly. He looked as bluff as bull beef.
An inn-keeper. Cant.
A short gun, with a wide bore, for carrying slugs; also a stupid, blundering fellow.
Money. Cant.
To talk big, to hector or bully.
Bridewell, Newgate, or any other prison, or house of correction.
A shoplifter's assistant, or one that receives and carries off stolen goods. All is bob; all is safe. Cant.
A shilling.
Cheated, tricked, disappointed.
Smart, clever, spruce.
Bum bailiffs.

entries.word: BODY OF DIVINITY BOUND IN BLACK CALF
entries.text: A parson.
Ask bogy, i.e. ask mine a-se. Sea wit.

Said to be the name of a Danish general, who so terrified his opponent Foh, that he caused him to bewray himself. Whence, when we smell a stink, it is custom to exclaim, Foh! i.e. I smell general Foh. He cannot say Boh to a goose; i.e. he is a cowardly or sheepish fellow. There is a story related of the celebrated Ben Jonson, who always dressed very plain; that being introduced to the presence of a nobleman, the peer, struck by his homely appearance and awkward manner, exclaimed, as if in doubt, "you Ben Johnson! why you look as if you could not say Boh to a goose!" "Boh!" replied the wit.
Bold as a miller's shirt, which every day takes a rogue by the collar.
A blunt arrow.
As erect, or straight up, as an arrow set on its end.

To run suddenly out of one's house, or hiding place, through fear; a term borrowed from a rabbit-warren, where the rabbits are made to bolt, by sending ferrets into their burrows: we set the house on fire, and made him bolt. To bolt, also means to swallow meat without chewing: the farmer's servants in Kent are famous for bolting large quantities of pickled pork.
Dice.
The mouth. Shut your bone box; shut your mouth.
A footman.
Seized, apprehended, taken up by a constable. CANT.
A nick name for an apothecary.
A hard-trotting horse.
A one-horse chaise, noddy, buggy, or leathern bottle.
Cards to play with. To plant the books; to place the cards in the pack in an unfair manner.
One who never returns borrowed books. Out of one's books; out of one's fevor. Out of his books; out of debt.
The servant at an inn whose business it is to clean the boots of the guest.
To play booty; cheating play, where the player purposely avoids winning.
One who sometimes hides himself, and sometimes appears publicly abroad, is said to-play at bo-peep. Also one who lies perdue, or on the watch.
A skin for holding wine, commonly a goat's; also a nick name for a drunkard.
A shilling. A half borde; a sixpence.

entries.word: BORN UNDER A THREEPENNY HALFPENNY PLANET
entries.text: NEVER TO BE WORTH A GROAT. Said of any person remarkably unsuccessful in his attempts or profession.
A nick name for a taylor.
A convivial society.
Void of wit.

A polite term for the posteriors. Also, in the sporting sense, strength and spirits to support fatigue; as a bottomed horse. Among bruisers it is used to express a hardy fellow, who will bear a good beating.
He is up in the boughs; he is in a passion.
A bottle; from the explosion in drawing the cork. CANT.
A purse. CANT.
A cut purse. CANT.--Formerly purses were worn at the girdle, from whence they were cut.
Drink.
Drunk.
An ale-house or gin-shop.
The nose, from its being the most projecting part of the human face, as the bowsprit is of a ship.
Dog's flesh.
A salesman's shop in Monmouth-street; so called because the servant barks, and the master bites. See BARKER.
One that draws a long bow, a dealer in the marvellous, a teller of improbable stories, a liar: perhaps from the wonderful shots frequently boasted of by archers.
To say or repeat the mariner's compass, not only backwards or forwards, but also to be able to answer any and all questions respecting its divisions. SEA TERM.
Mead and ale sweetened with honey.
vain-glorious fellow, a boaster.
Red-faced, as if from drinking brandy.
Brandy is Latin for a goose; a memento to prevent the animal from rising in the stomach by a glass of the good creature.

A vicar of Bray; one who frequently changes his principles, always siding with the strongest party: an allusion to a vicar of Bray, in Berkshire, commemorated in a well-known ballad for the pliability of his conscience.
Bold-faced, shameless, impudent.
Hard words, difficult to pronounce.
Borrowing money; perhaps from the figurative operation being, like the real one, extremely disagreeable to the patient.
Employment. Out of bread; out of employment. In bad bread; in a disagreeable scrape, or situation.
The stomach; a term used by boxers. I took him a punch in his bread basket; i.e. I gave him a blow in the stomach.
An edition of the Bible printed in 1598, wherein it is said that Adam and Eve sewed figleaves together, and made themselves breeches.
To raise a breeze; to kick up a dust or breed a disturbance.
To make a bridge of any one's nose; to push the bottle past him, so as to deprive him of his turn of filling his glass; to pass one over. Also to play booty, or purposely to avoid winning.
Porter.
A soldier BUSKIN. A player. BUNG. A brewer QUILL. An author. STRING. A fiddler. WHIP. A coachman.
A boxer: a disciple of Broughton, who was a beef-eater, and once the best boxer of his day.
A soldier's firelock. To hug brown Bess; to carry a firelock, or serve as a private soldier.
An ammunition loaf, A wig without powder; similar to the undress wig worn by his majesty.
Said of one absent, in a reverie, or thoughtful.
A boxer; one skilled in the art of boxing also an inferior workman among chasers.
The fat scum from the pot in which salted beef is boiled.
A bumper, a full glass. See BUMPER.
Strong beer.
A drinking bowl; also a great drinker; a thief that steals plate from public houses. CANT.
The party cheated, perhaps from his being like an air bubble, filled with words, which are only wind, instead of real property.
To cheat.
To except against the general rule, that he who lays the odds must always be adjudged the loser: this is restricted to betts laid for liquor.
Beef and cabbage fried together. It is so called from its bubbling up and squeaking whilst over the fire.
Bail given by a sharper for one of the gang.
To kick the bucket; to die.
Fetters.

One that slips into houses in the dark, to steal cloaks or other clothes. Also lambs' fur formerly used for doctors' robes, whence they were called budge doctors. Standing budge; a thief's scout or spy.
To move, or quit one's station. Don't budge from hence; i.e. don't move from hence, stay here.

A wallet. To open the budget; a term used to signify the notification of the taxes required by the minister for the expences of the ensuing year; as To-morrow the minister will go to the house, and open the budget.
A dog. Bufe's nob; a dog's head. CANT.
A dog stealer. CANT.
To stand buff; to stand the brunt. To swear as a witness. He buffed it home; and I was served; he swore hard against me, and I was found guilty.
Confused, stupid.

A cant word among journeymen hatters, signifying the exchanging some of the dearest materials of which a hat is made for others of less value. Hats are composed of the furs and wool of divers animals among which is a small portion of beavers' fur. Bugging, is stealing the beaver, and substituting in lieu thereof an equal weight of some cheaper ingredient.--Bailiffs who take money to postpone or refrain the serving of a writ, are said to bug the writ.
An upholsterer.
A scare-babe, or bully-beggar.
A one-horse chaise.
Two pickpockets; the bulk jostles the party to be robbed, and the file does the business.
One who lodges all night on a bulk or projection before old-fashioned shop windows.
A crown piece. A half bull; half a crown.
A great hulkey or clumsy fellow. See HULKEY.
Pistols.
Persons who over-drive bulls, or frequent bull baits.
A crown-piece.
To hector, bounce, or bully.
A cowardly fellow, who gives himself airs of great bravery. A bully huff cap; a hector. See HECTOR.
Highwaymen who attack passengers with paths and imprecations.
the breech, or backside.
To arrest a debtor. The gill bummed the swell for a thimble; the tradesman arrested the gentleman for a watch.
A sheriff's officer who arrests debtors. Ware hawke! the bum traps are fly to our panney; keep a good look out, the bailiffs know where our house is situated.

A sheriff's officer, who arrests debtors; so called perhaps from following his prey, and being at their bums, or, as the vulgar phrase is, hard at their a-ses. Blackstone says, it is a corruption of bound bailiff, from their being obliged to give bond for their good behaviour.
Soft paper for the necessary house or torchecul.
The backside, the breech. See ARS MUSICA.
A raw country fellow.
Arrested.
A full glass; in all likelihood from its convexity or bump at the top: some derive it from a full glass formerly drunk to the health of the pope--AU BON PERE.
Said of a person lying on his face.
Drink a dram; strictly speaking, to drink till one's eye is bunged up or closed.
An apron.
A jocular name for a baker.
Strollers living in an alehouse without paying their quarters, are said to burn the ken. CANT.
He is no burner of navigable rivers; i.e. he is no conjuror, or man of extraordinary abilities; or rather, he is, but a simple fellow. See THAMES.
A constable. CANT.
A watchman. CANT.
As busy is the devil in a high wind; as busy as a hen with one chick.
That must have been a butcher's horse, by his carrying a calf so well; a vulgar joke on an awkward rider.
A dependant, poor relation, or simpleton, on whom all kinds of practical jokes are played off; and who serves as a butt for all the shafts of wit and ridicule.
A bad shilling, among coiners. His a-se makes buttons; he is ready to bewray himself through fear. CANT.
A pickpocket. CANT.
A sh-te-fire, a furious braggadocio or bully huff.
To blab, or discover secrets. The cull is leaky, and cackles; the rogue tells all. CANT. See LEAKY.
A hen.
A hen roost. CANT.
Fowls. CANT.
Eggs. CANT.
A helper. An under-strapper.
To beg. Cadge the swells; beg of the gentlemen.
Cheese. CANT.
To be cagged. To be sulky or out of humour. The cove carries the cag; the man is vexed or sullen.
Bits and scraps of provisions. Bad meat.
A foolish fellow.

A drum. To smack calf's skin; to kiss the book in taking an oath. It is held by the St. Giles's casuists, that by kissing one's thumb instead of smacking calf's skin, the guilt of taking a false oath is avoided.
Rum and spruce beer, American beverage.
A cloak or gown. CANT.
A willow.
A bottle, or soldier's bayonet.
The hulks or lighters, on board of which felons are condemned to hard labour. Mr. Campbell was the first director of them. See ACADEMY and FLOATING ACADEMY.
Bad, small, or untunable bells. Hark! how the candlesticks rattle.
To lay Cane upon Abel; to beat any one with a cane or stick.
The head. To mill his cannister; to break his head.
A small can: also, in the canting sense, the plague.
An hypocrite, a double-tongue palavering fellow. See PALAVER.
To cant; to toss or throw: as, Cant a slug into your bread room; drink a dram. SEA WIT.
A parish clerk.
A long roundabout tale.
To take one's oath. I will cap downright; I will swear home. CANT.

To take off one's hat or cap. To cap the quadrangle; a lesson of humility, or rather servility, taught undergraduates at the university, where they are obliged to cross the area of the college cap in hand, in reverence to the fellows who sometimes walk there. The same ceremony is observed on coming on the quarter deck of ships of war, although no officer should be on it.

To support another's assertion or tale. To assist a man in cheating. The file kidded the joskin with sham books, and his pall capped; the deep one cheated the countryman with false cards, and his confederate assisted in the fraud.
Repeating Latin Verses in turn, beginning with the letter with which the last speaker left off.
To overturn or reverse. He took his broth till he capsized; he drank till he fell out of his chair. SEA TERM.
All officers; a saying of a company where everyone strives to rule.

Meat between veal and beef, the flesh of an old calf; a military simile, drawn from the officer of that denomination, who has only the pay of a lieutenant, with the rank of captain; and so is not entirely one or the other, but between both.
A celebrated master of a puppet-shew, in Ben Johnson's time, whose name became a common one to signify any of that fraternity.
A shabby ill-dressed fellow.
A cheating bully, or one in a set of gamblers, whose office is to bully any pigeon, who, suspecting roguery, refuses to pay what he has lost. CANT.
The leader of a mob; also the mob itself.
A large sum of money; also, a person cheated of such sum. CANT.
A cloak in fashion about the year 1760.
A set of rogues who are employed to look out and watch upon the roads, at inns, &c. in order to carry information to their respective gangs, of a booty in prospect.
Pigeons which carry expresses.
An undertaker; called also a cold cook, and death hunter. See COLD COOK and DEATH HUNTER.
A sort of conundrum, puzzlewit, or riddle.
To vomit.
Cheese; CANT. See CAFFAN.
A cloak. CANT.
A hat. To prig a castor; to steal a hat.
Vomiting.

entries.word: TO CAT, or SHOOT THE CAT
entries.text: To vomit from drunkenness.
A society which met at their office in the great western road: in their summons, published in the daily papers, it was added, that the kittens might come with the old cats without being scratched.

A kind of whistle, chiefly used at theatres, to interrupt the actors, and damn a new piece. It derives its name from one of its sounds, which greatly resembles the modulation of an intriguing boar cat.
Drinking cross-ways, and not, as usual, over the left thumb. SEA TERM.
To turn cat in pan, to change sides or parties; supposed originally to have been to turn CATE or CAKE in pan.
Tea, called also scandal broth. See SCANDAL BROTH.
When a rook or cully is engaged amongst bad bowlers.
A scourge composed of nine strings of whip-cord, each string having nine knots.

To be made a cat's paw of; to be made a tool or instrument to accomplish the purpose of another: an allusion to the story of a monkey, who made use of a cat's paw to scratch a roasted chesnut out of the fire.
Counterfeit sleep: cats often counterfeiting sleep, to decoy their prey near them, and then suddenly spring on them.

entries.word: CAT WHIPPING, or WHIPPING THE CAT
entries.text: A trick often practised on ignorant country fellows, vain of their strength, by laying a wager with them that they may be pulled through a pond by a cat. The bet being made, a rope is fixed round the waist of the party to be catted, and the end thrown across the pond, to which the cat is also fastened by a packthread, and three or four sturdy fellows are appointed to lead and whip the cat; these on a signal given, seize the end of the cord, and pretending to whip the cat, haul the astonished booby through the water.--To whip the cat, is also a term among tailors for working jobs at private houses, as practised in the country.
Any temporary contrivance to raise a contribution on the public.
A bum bailiff, or sheriff's officer.
A dangerous time for a robbery, when many persons are on the road, on account of a horse-race, fair, or some other public meeting.
Good friends. He and I are not cater cousins, i.e. we are not even cousins in the fourth degree, or four times removed; that is, we have not the least friendly connexion.

A nick name for a soldier. In the year 1745, a soldier quartered at a house near Derby, was desired by his landlord to call upon him, whenever he came that way; for, added he, soldiers are the pillars of the nation. The rebellion being finished, it happened the same regiment was quartered in Derbyshire, when the soldier resolved to accept of his landlord's invitation, and accordingly obtained leave to go to him: but, on his arrival, he was greatly surprised to find a very cold reception; whereupon expostulating with his landlord, he reminded him of his invitation, and the circumstance of his having said, soldiers were the pillars of the nation. If I did, answered the host, I meant CATERpiliars.
Old-fashioned. An old cathedral-bedstead, chair, &c.
Left-handed.
Awkward, not dextrous, ready, or nimble.
An old weather-beaten wig.
An usurer.
Well beaten; from CHAUFFE, warmed.
The amusement above described.
A fellow; An odd chap; A strange fellow.
Dry or thirsty.
Burnt in the hand. They have palmed the character upon him; they have burned him in the hand, CANT.--See LETTERED.
A picklock. CANT.
Tea. See CAT LAP and SCANDAL BROTH.
The gallows. CANT.
Grub-street writers, who compose songs, carrols, &c. for ballad-singers. CANT.
A song.
To sing. To publish an account in the newspapers. The kiddey was chaunted for a toby; his examination concerning a highway robbery was published in the papers.
A countryman. A stupid fellow.
He came at it by way of Cheapside; he gave little or nothing for it, he bought it cheap.
Sham sleeves to put over a dirty shift or shirt. See SHAMS.
Side by side, hand to fist.
A sword.
Be silent, be quiet, don't do it. Cheese it, the coves are fly; be silent, the people understand our discourse.
A strong smelling fart.

A village near London, famous for the military hospital. To get Chelsea; to obtain the benefit of that hospital. Dead Chelsea, by G-d! an exclamation uttered by a grenadier at Fontenoy, on having his leg carried away by a cannon-ball.
A black cat, there being black cherries as well as red.
He grins like a Cheshire cat; said of anyone who shews his teeth and gums in laughing.
A poulterer.
Fearful, cowardly.
One returned from the East Indies with but a moderate fortune of fifty or sixty thousand pounds, a diminutive nabob: a term borrowed from the chicken turtle.
A brother chip; a person of the same trade or calling.
A nick name for a carpenter.
Exhilarated with liquor. Chirping glass, a cheerful glass, that makes the company chirp like birds in spring.
The bowels. There is a rumpus among my bowels, i.e. I have the colic. The frill of a shirt.
Baby-faced; said of one who has a childish look.
I gave him a good chivey; I gave him, a hearty Scolding.
Cutting the braces of coaches behind, on which the coachman quitting the box, an accomplice robs the boot; also, formerly, cutting the back of the coach to steal the fine large wigs then worn.

Choak away, the churchyard's near; a jocular saying to a person taken with a violent fit of coughing, or who has swallowed any thing, as it is called the wrong way; Choak, chicken, more are hatching: a like consolation.

A punishment inflicted on any person sleeping in company: it consists in wrapping up cotton in a case or tube of paper, setting it on fire, and directing the smoke up the nostrils of the sleeper. See HOWELL'S COTGRAVE.
To give chocolate without sugar; to reprove. MILITARY TERM.
A thoughtless, laughing, singing, drunken fellow.
A blow. Boxing term.

To exchange backwards and forwards. To chop, in the canting sense, means making dispatch, or hurrying over any business: ex. The AUTEM BAWLER will soon quit the HUMS, for he CHOPS UP the WHINERS; the parson will soon quit the pulpit, for he hurries over the prayers. See AUTEM BAWLER, HUMS, and WHINERS,
Simoniacal dealers in livings, or other ecclesiastical preferments.
The mouth. I gave him a wherrit, or a souse, across the chops; I gave him a blow over the mouth, See WHERRIT.
A fork.
A sea-dish, composed of fresh fish, salt pork, herbs, and sea-biscuits, laid in different layers, and stewed together.
To cheat or trick: he choused me out of it. Chouse is also the term for a game like chuck-farthing.
Erasing the name of the true maker from a stolen watch, and engraving a fictitious one in its place.
A chairman.
A cough, kibed heels, and a snotty nose.
He is a young chub, or a mere chub; i.e. a foolish fellow, easily imposed on: an illusion to a fish of that name, easily taken.
Round-faced, plump.
My chuck; a term of endearment.
A parish clerk.
Stupid, thick-headed.
Round-faced, chubby.
A chamber-fellow, particularly at the universities and in prison.

Money paid by the richer sort of prisoners in the Fleet and King's Bench, to the poorer, for their share of a room. When prisons are very full, which is too often the case, particularly on the eve of an insolvent act, two or three persons are obliged to sleep in a room. A prisoner who can pay for being alone, chuses two poor chums, who for a stipulated price, called chummage, give up their share of the room, and sleep on the stairs, or, as the term is, ruff it.
Among printers, a journeyman who refuses to work for legal wages; the same as the flint among taylors. See FLINT.
A Sussex name for a shag, or cormorant, probably from its voracity.
Said of any work that advances slowly.
A cough that is likely to terminate in death.
Originally, a labourer or husbandman: figuratively a rude, surly, boorish fellow. To put a churl upon a gentleman; to drink malt liquor immediately after having drunk wine.
A roundabout way, or story. He took such a circumbendibus; he took such a circuit.
A citizen of London.
Newgate.
A reward claimed by bailiffs for executing their office with civility.
A pulpit, so called by orator Henley.
Starved.
A silver tankard. CANT.
A silver tankard stealer. See RUM BUBBER.
A great lie.
Very drunk. The cull is clear, let's bite him; the fellow is very drunk, let's cheat him. CANT.
Expert; clever. Amongst the knuckling coves he is reckoned very clean; he is considered very expert as a pickpocket.
Soothed, funned, imposed on. The cull will not be clerked; i.e. the fellow will not be imposed on by fair words.
Artificial sores, made by beggars to excite charity.
A blow. A click in the muns; a blow or knock in the face. CANT.
To snatch. To click a nab; to snatch a hat. CANT.
A salesman's servant; also, one who proportions out the different shares of the booty among thieves.
To climb the three trees with a ladder; to ascend the gallows.

A pun or quibble. To clinch, or to clinch the nail; to confirm an improbable story by another: as, A man swore he drove a tenpenny nail through the moon; a bystander said it was true, for he was on the other side and clinched it.

A place in the Borough of Southwark, formerly privileged from arrests; and inhabited by lawless vagabonds of every denomination, called, from the place of their residence, clinkers. Also a gaol, from the clinking of the prisoners' chains or fetters: he is gone to clink.
To hug or embrace: to clip and cling. To clip the coin; to diminish the current coin. To clip the king's English; to be unable to speak plain through drunkenness.
Rogues who lurk about the entrances into dark alleys, and bye-lanes, to snatch cloaks from the shoulders of passengers.
A country farmer, or ploughman.
A dull, heavy booby.
The same.
Covetous or stingy.
He is just come from the cloth market, i.e. from between the sheets, he is just risen from bed.
Tobacco. Under a cloud; in adversity.

To spy the cloven foot in any business; to discover some roguery or something bad in it: a saying that alludes to a piece of vulgar superstition, which is, that, let the Devil transform himself into what shape he will, he cannot hide his cloven foot
Shoes tipped with iron.
To be, or live, in clover; to live luxuriously. Clover is the most desirable food for cattle.
Rogues.
To steal. To cloy the clout; to steal the handkerchief. To cloy the lour; to steal money. CANT.
Thieves, robbers, &c.
A meeting or association, where each man is to spend an equal and stated sum, called his club.
Argumentum bacculinum, in which an oaken stick is a better plea than an act of parliament.
A lump. Clumpish; lumpish, stupid.
An awkward clownish fellow.
To clench or shut the hand. Clutch fisted; covetous, stingy. See CLOSE-FISTED.
Hands, gripe, power.
A stir, noise, or racket: what a confounded clutter here is!
To be whipped. CANT.
A nick name for an apothecary.
A half crown piece is a fore coach wheel, and a crown piece a hind coach wheel; the fore wheels of a coach being less than the hind ones.

To fondle, or wheedle. To coax a pair of stockings; to pull down the part soiled into the shoes, so as to give a dirty pair of stockings the appearance of clean ones. Coaxing is also used, instead of darning, to hide the holes about the ancles.
A kind of boat.
To mend, or patch; likewise to do a thing in a bungling manner.
A turkey.
A mender of shoes, an improver of the understandings of his customers; a translator.
Treacle, vinegar, gin, and water.
A cod of money: a good sum of money.
Persons employed by the gardeners to gather peas.
An old codger: an old fellow.
A stupid fellow.
The money, or whatsoever the sweeteners drop to draw in a bubble.
A tooth. A queer cog; a rotten tooth. How the cull flashes his queer cogs; how the fool shews his rotten teeth.
To cheat with dice; also to coax or wheedle, To cog a die; to conceal or secure a die. To cog a dinner; to wheedle one out of a dinner.
A dram of any spirituous liquor.
A lie.
The fool in the play of Bartholomew Fair: perhaps a contraction of the word COXCOMB.

A punishment inflicted by private soldiers on their comrades for trifling offences, or breach of their mess laws; it is administered in the following manner: The prisoner is set against the wall, with the arm which is to be burned tied as high above his head as possible. The executioner then ascends a stool, and having a bottle of cold water, pours it slowly down the sleeve of the delinquent, patting him, and leading the water gently down his body, till it runs out at his breeches knees: this is repeated to the other arm, if he is sentenced to be burned in both.
An undertaker of funerals, or carrion hunter. See CARRION HUNTER.
A sword, or any other weapon for cutting or stabbing. I gave him two inches of cold iron into his beef.
Money. Post the cole: pay down the money.
Money.
Execution day.

Newgate or any other prison. New College: the Royal Exchange. King's College: the King's Bench prison. He has been educated at the steel, and took his last degree at college; he has received his education at the house of correction, and was hanged at Newgate.

The College cove has numbered him, and if he is knocked down he'll be twisted; the turnkey of Newgate has told the judge how many times the prisoner has been tried before and therefore if he is found guilty, he certainly will be hanged. It is said to be the custom of the Old Bailey for one of the turnkeys of Newgate to give information to the judge how many times an old offender has been tried, by holding up as many fingers as the number of times the prisoner has been before arraigned at that bar.
Prisoners of the one, and shopkeepers of the other of those places.
A highwayman.
To wheedle or coax.
who roasted the devil in his feathers. A bad cook.
A shroud.
Brandy.
Wine and water, with lemon, sugar, and burrage.
A man's neck. His colquarron is just about to be twisted; he is just going to be hanged. CANT.
One who lets horses to highwaymen; also a boy newly initiated into roguery; a grand or petty juryman on his first assize. CANT.
A fine or beverage paid by colts on their first entering into their offices.
Laid short of the jack by a colt bowler, i.e. a person raw or unexperienced in the art of bowling.
Coarse red veal, more like the flesh of a colt than that of a calf.
A shirt. CANT.
The house of commons; the necessary house.
See CHRISTMAS.
A social meeting formerly held at the Half Moon tavern Cheapside.
Counterfeited.

To conger; the agreement of a set or knot of booksellers of London, that whosoever of them shall buy a good copy, the rest shall take off such a particular number, in quires, at a stated price; also booksellers joining to buy either a considerable or dangerous copy.
Will you lap your congo with me? will you drink tea with me?
A superior, who by his influence makes his dependants act as he pleases.
The cull's content; the man is past complaining: a saying of a person murdered for resisting the robbers. CANT.
A thick liquor, in imitation of chocolate, made of milk and gingerbread.
A dance where the dancers of the different sexes stand opposite each other, instead of side by side, as in the minuet, rigadoon, louvre, &c. and now corruptly called a country dance.
Enigmatical conceits.
A necessary. A leathern conveniency, a coach.
Imprisoned, confined like a fowl in a coop.
Light-headed, foolish.
Drunk.
A large belly. He has a glorious corporation; he has a very prominent belly.
The magistrates, &c. of a corporate town. Corpus sine ratione. Freemen of a corporation's work; neither strong nor handsome.
A foundling. Cosset colt or lamb; a colt or lamb brought up by hand.
The head. I'll smite your costard; I'll give you a knock on the head.
A dealer in fruit, particularly apples.
A man, a fellow, a rogue. The cove was bit; the rogue was outwitted. The cove has bit the cole; the rogue has got the money. CANT.

To send one to Coventry; a punishment inflicted by officers of the army on such of their brethren as are testy, or have been guilty of improper behaviour, not worthy the cognizance of a court martial. The person sent to Coventry is considered as absent; no one must speak to or answer any question he asks, except relative to duty, under penalty of being also sent to the same place. On a proper submission, the penitent is recalled, and welcomed by the mess, as just returned from a journey to Coventry.
To lie down to sleep. CANT.
A waggoner. CANT.
An ignorant country fellow.
Said of any work that advances slowly.
COURT PROMISES. Fair speeches and promises, without performance.
Milk.
A calf.
Gallop and sh---e.
Awkward.
Fearful.
The product of a sort of bean, which excites an insufferable itching, used chiefly for playing tricks.
A bull.
Done to a cow's thumb; done exactly.
To catch a crab; to fall backwards by missing one's stroke in rowing.
A peevish fellow.
A losing throw to the main at hazard.
Sour, ill-tempered, difficult.
To boast or brag; also to break. I cracked his napper; I broke his head.

entries.word: THE CRACK, or ALL THE CRACK
entries.text: The fashionable theme, the go. The Crack Lay, of late is used, in the cant language, to signify the art and mystery of house-breaking.
Crust, sea biscuit, or ammunition loaf; also the backside. Farting crackers; breeches.
Implements of house-breaking, such as a crow, a center bit, false keys, &c.

Hedges. The cull thought to have loped by breaking through the crackmans, but we fetched him back by a nope on the costard, which stopped his jaw; the man thought to have escaped by breaking through the hedge, but we brought him back by a great blow on the head, which laid him speechless.
A house-breaker. The kiddy is a clever cracksman; the young fellow is a very expert house-breaker.
The neck.
Bolts, shackles, or fetters. CANT.
Sentence of death passed on a criminal by a judge. He has just undergone the cramp word; sentence has just been passed on him. CANT.
Gin and water; also, brisk, pert.
To kill. Crash that cull; kill that fellow. CANT.
Teeth.
Such as young fellows pretend to dairymaids, to get cream and other good things from them.
To slip or slide any thing into the hands of another. CANT.
Gentlemen's companions, lice.
A house. To crack a crib: to break open a house.
To purloin, or appropriate to one's own use, part of any thing intrusted to one's care.
To make a sham fight. BEAR GARDEN TERM.
Every Monday throughout the year, but most particularly the 25th of October, being the anniversary of Crispinus and Crispianus.
An awl.
One who is always foretelling some accident or misfortune: an allusion to the croaking of a raven, supposed ominous.
Forestallers, called also Kidders and Tranters.
The tears of a hypocrite. Crocodiles are fabulously reported to shed tears over their prey before they devour it.
A nick name for a surgeon of the army and navy.
A groat, or four pence.
An intimate companion, a comrade; also a confederate in a robbery.
Sixpence.
To crook one's elbow, and wish it may never come straight, if the fact then affirmed is not true--according to the casuists of Bow-street and St. Giles's, adds great weight and efficacy to an oath.
To be knocked down for a crop; to be condemned to be hanged. Cropped, hanged.
Drummers of the foot guards, or Chelsea hospital, who find out weddings, and beat a point of war to serenade the new married couple, and thereby obtain money.
Sickness in the stomach, arising from drunkenness.
To come home by weeping cross; to repent at the conclusion.
A cross cove; any person who lives by stealing or in a dishonest manner.
A fiddle: probably from CROOTH, the Welch name for that instrument.
A fiddler.
Oatmeal and water, or milk; a mess much eaten in the north.
A visitation of the clergy. See REVIEW OF THE BLACK CUIRASSIERS.
Beggars, or highway spies, who traverse the road, to give intelligence of a booty; also rogues ready to snap up any booty that may offer, like privateers or pirates on a cruise.
A surly fellow.

An unlicked cub; an unformed, ill-educated young man, a young nobleman or gentleman on his travels: an allusion to the story of the bear, said to bring its cub into form by licking. Also, a new gamester.
Taylors, who are jocularly said to subsist, during the summer, chiefly on cucumbers.
A man.
A man, honest or otherwise. A bob cull; a good-natured, quiet fellow. CANT.
A disposition liable to be cheated, an unsuspecting nature, open to imposition.
A punning appellation for a simple fellow.
A sharp fellow, one that trims close, i.e. cheats ingeniously.
A cup of good liquor.
Drunk.
Pretended love to the cook, or any other person, for the sake of a meal. My guts cry cupboard; i.e. I am hungry
The act of hooking goods out of windows: the curber is the thief, the curb the hook. CANT.
A dyachilon plaister, applied to the parts galled by riding.
Clippings of money, which curls up in the operation. CANT.
To curry favour; to obtain the favour of a person be coaxing or servility. To curry any one's hide; to beat him.
Broken petty-fogging attornies, or Newgate solicitors. CANT.
A parson; many of whom in the fury of their eloquence, heartily belabour their cushions.
The cap worn by the sword-bearer of the city of London, made hollow at the top like a custard.
Drunk. A little cut over the head; slightly intoxicated. To cut; to leave a person or company. To cut up well; to die rich.

(Cambridge.) To renounce acquaintance with any one is to CUT him. There are several species of the CUT. Such as the cut direct, the cut indirect, the cut sublime, the cut infernal, &c. The cut direct, is to start across the street, at the approach of the obnoxious person in order to avoid him. The cut indirect, is to look another way, and pass without appearing to observe him. The cut sublime, is to admire the top of King's College Chapel, or the beauty of the passing clouds, till he is out of sight. The cut infernal, is to analyze the arrangement of your shoe-strings, for the same purpose.
To speak gently. To cut bene whiddes; to give good words. To cut queer whiddes; to give foul language. To cut a bosh, or a flash; to make a figure. CANT.
To look out of the corners of one's eyes, to leer, to look askance. The cull cutty-eyed at us; the fellow looked suspicious at us.
Two pence. Tip me a dace; lend me two pence. CANT.
Hands. Tip us your daddle; give me your hand. CANT.
Father. Old daddy; a familiar address to an old man. To beat daddy mammy; the first rudiments of drum beating, being the elements of the roll.
They are at daggers drawing; i.e. at enmity, ready to fight.
A jockey term for a horse that does not lift up his legs sufficiently, or goes too near the ground, and is therefore apt to stumble.
Ostlers at great inns.
A rascal. See DIMBER.
A roaring, mad, blustering fellow, a scourer of the streets, or kicker up of a breeze.

A clerk in a counting house, whose sole business it is to clear or swear off merchandise at the custom-house; and who, it is said, guards against the crime of perjury, by taking a previous oath, never to swear truly on those occasions.
A luncheon, or snap before dinner: so called from its damping, or allaying, the appetite; eating and drinking, being, as the proverb wisely observes, apt to take away the appetite.
To be hanged.
Stairs.
That's the dandy; i.e. the ton, the clever thing; an expression of similar import to "That's the barber." See BARBER.
A dirty brown. His coat's dandy grey russet, the colour of the Devil's nutting bag.
An insignificant or trifling fellow.
A smart, well-made, little man.
Fetters. CANT.
Ready money. CANT.
The night. CANT.
One that slides into a house in the dark of the evening, and hides himself, in order to let some of the gang in at night to rob it.
A straight-armed blow in boxing.
A tavern drawer. To cut a dash: to make a figure.
The devil, the spirit of the sea: called Necken in the north countries, such as Norway, Denmark, and Sweden.
The sea.
I'll take my davy of it; vulgar abbreviation of affidavit.
To bribe. The cull was scragged because he could not dawb; the rogue was hanged because he could not bribe. All bedawbed with lace; all over lace.
Eyes. To darken his day lights, or sow up his sees; to close up a man's eyes in boxing.
A term used by thieves, when they are disappointed in the value of their booty.
To work for the dead horse; to work for wages already paid.
Vulgar pronunciation of the Dedalus ship of war.
A cant word among journeymen bakers, for loaves falsely charged to their masters' customers; also empty bottles.
that bears fruit all the year round. The gallows, or three-legged mare. See THREE-LEGGED MARE.
An undertaker, one who furnishes the necessary articles for funerals. See CARRION HUNTER.
A poor miserable, emaciated fellow; one quite an otomy. See OTOMY.--He looked as pleasant as the pains of death.
A thorough-paced rogue, a sly designing fellow: in opposition to a shallow or foolish one.
A neat little man.
To come down with the derbies; to pay the money.

The name of the finisher of the law, or hangman about the year 1608.--'For he rides his circuit with the Devil, and Derrick must be his host, and Tiburne the inne at which he will lighte.' Vide Bellman of London, in art. PRIGGIN LAW.--'At the gallows, where I leave them, as to the haven at which they must all cast anchor, if Derrick's cables do but hold.' Ibid.
The gizzard of a turkey or fowl, scored, peppered, salted and broiled: it derives its appellation from being hot in the mouth.
Cards.
A parson. See SNUB DEVIL.
A miserable painter.
Assafoetida.
A surveyor's chain: so called by farmers, who do not like their land should be measured by their landlords.

Very: an epithet which in the English vulgar language is made to agree with every quality or thing; as, devilish bad, devilish good; devilish sick, devilish well; devilish sweet, devilish sour; devilish hot, devilish cold, &c. &c.
The country. Cant.
Country carriers. Cant.
Feet. Cant.
Two-pence. Cant.
Torn to pieces by a mob, as that great statesman John de Wit was in Holland, anno 1672.
The face. To alter his dial plate; to disfigure his face.

The names of false dice: A bale of bard cinque deuces A bale of flat cinque deuces A bale of flat sice aces A bale of bard cater traes A bale of flat cater traes A bale of fulhams A bale of light graniers A bale of langrets contrary to the ventage A bale of gordes, with as many highmen as lowmen, for passage A bale of demies A bale of long dice for even and odd A bale of bristles A bale of direct contraries.
That happened in the reign of queen Dick, i. e. never: said of any absurd old story. I am as queer as Dick's hatband; that is, out of spirits, or don't know what ails me.
A sham shirt.
An ass. Roll your dickey; drive your ass. Also a seat for servants to sit behind a carriage, when their master drives.
To cheat. To defraud. The cull diddled me out of my dearee; the fellow robbed me of my sweetheart. See Jeremy Diddler In Raising The Wind.
Gin.
Spurs. Cant.
Small pieces of excrement adhering to the hairs near the fundament.
The fundament.
Double diligent, like the Devil's apothecary; said of one affectedly diligent.
A top man, or prince, among the canting crew: also the chief rogue of the gang, or the completest cheat. CANT.

To knock down. To ding it in one's ears; to reproach or tell one something one is not desirous of hearing. Also to throw away or hide: thus a highwayman who throws away or hides any thing with which he robbed, to prevent being known or detected, is, in the canting lingo, styled a Dinger.
A rogue, a hector, a bully, or sharper. CANT.
Helter skelter, in a hasty disorderly manner.

A mode of stealing in houses that let lodgings, by rogues pretending to be postmen, who send up sham letters to the lodgers, and, whilst waiting in the entry for the postage, go into the first room they see open, and rob it.

To dip for a wig. Formerly, in Middle Row, Holborn, wigs of different sorts were, it is said, put into a close-stool box, into which, for three-pence, any one might dip, or thrust in his hand, and take out the first wig he laid hold of; if he was dissatisfied with his prize, he might, on paying three halfpence, return it and dip again.
A cook's shop, under Furnival's Inn, where many attornies clerks, and other inferior limbs of the law, take out the wrinkles from their bellies. DIP is also a punning name for a tallow-chandler.
Pawned or mortgaged.
Drunk.
Offended, disobliged.
He is completely dished up; he is totally ruined. To throw a thing in one's dish; to reproach or twit one with any particular matter.
The psalm sung by the felons at the gallows, just before they are turned off.
A mittimus, or justice of the peace's warrant, for the commitment of a rogue.
A suit of ditto; coat, waistcoat, and breeches, all of one colour.
Loaded or false dice.
A pickpocket; also one who lives in a cellar.
Carries the same meaning, but is not so briefly expressed: the former having received the polish of the present times.
A cloak. Cant.
Milk and water, with a little rum, and some nutmeg; also the name of a composition used by distillers, to make spirits appear stronger than they really are, or, in their phrase, better proof.
Loaded dice, that will run but two or three chances. They put the doctors upon him; they cheated him with loaded dice.
Dog stealers, who kill those dogs not advertised for, sell their skins, and feed the remaining dogs with their flesh.

An old dog at it; expert or accustomed to any thing. Dog in a manger; one who would prevent another from enjoying what he himself does not want: an allusion to the well-known fable. The dogs have not dined; a common saying to any one whose shirt hangs out behind. To dog, or dodge; to follow at a distance. To blush like a blue dog, i.e. not at all. To walk the black dog on any one; a punishment inflicted in the night on a fresh prisoner, by his comrades, in case of his refusal to pay the usual footing or garnish.
Barbarous Latin, such as was formerly used by the lawyers in their pleadings.
Rain water.
Surly.
To reprove or command in an insolent or haughty manner. Don't think as how you shall domineer here.
Robbed: also, convicted or hanged. Cant.--See DO.
Ruined by gaming and extravagances. Modern Term.
A man's backside. Cotton's Virgil.
Roby Douglas, with one eye and a stinking breath; the breech. Sea wit.
Dice that run low.

Aware of a thing. Knowing it. There is NO DOWN. A cant phrase used by house-breakers to signify that the persons belonging to any house are not on their guard, or that they are fast asleep, and have not heard any noise to alarm them.
A blow in the face.
Vulgar pronunciation of DOUCEUR.
To go on the drag; to follow a cart or waggon, in order to rob it. CANT.
Waiting in the streets to rob carts or waggons.

A man who occupies two branches of one profession, is said to dragoon it; because, like the soldier of that denomination, he serves in a double capacity. Such is a physician who furnishes the medicines, and compounds his own prescriptions.
Gin: so called from the diuretic qualities imputed to that liquor.
A dram served upon credit.
An ale draper; an alehouse keeper.
ON THE PUMP AT ALDGATE. A bad or false bill of exchange. See ALDGATE.
Robbers of houses whose doors are only fastened with latches. CANT.
Stockings. CANT.
Coining. CANT.
To beat. I'll dress his hide neatly; I'll beat him soundly.
A method of pouring out, as it were, the dice from the box, gently, by which an old practitioner is enabled to cog one of them with his fore-finger.
A heavy, bungling thief or rogue. A purple dromedary; a bungler in the art and mystery of thieving. CANT.
See DOMMERER.
The new drop; a contrivance for executing felons at Newgate, by means of a platform, which drops from under them: this is also called the last drop. See LEAF. See MORNING DROP.
To let fall, with design, a piece of gold or silver, in order to draw in and cheat the person who sees it picked up; the piece so dropped is called a dropt cog.
Almost drunk.

Persons who practice the fraud of dropping a ring or other article, and picking it up before the person intended to be defrauded, they pretend that the thing is very valuable to induce their gull to lend them money, or to purchase the article. See FAWNY RIG, and MONEY DROPPERS.

To be dispirited. This expression is used by thieves to signify that their companion did not die game, as the kiddy dropped down when he went to be twisted; the young fellow was very low spirited when he walked out to be hanged.
To beat any one with a stick, or rope's end: perhaps a contraction of DRY RUB. It is also used to signify a good beating with any instrument.
A jockey term for a horse that throws about his fore legs irregularly: the idea is taken from a kettle drummer, who in beating makes many flourishes with his drumsticks.
Drunk as a wheel-barrow. Drunk as David's sow. See DAVID'S SOW.
A sly humorous fellow.
A picklock, or master-key. CANT.
Robbing houses by picking the locks.
Open the door. CANT.
A lick on the head.
A picker of locks. CANT.
Two-pence.

To make ducks and drakes: a school-boy's amusement, practised with pieces of tile, oyster-shells, or flattish stones, which being skimmed along the surface of a pond, or still river, rebound many times. To make ducks and drakes of one's money; to throw it idly away.

Cheats who travel the country, pretending to sell smuggled goods: they accost their intended dupes in a whisper. The goods they have for sale are old shop-keepers, or damaged; purchased by them of large manufactories. See DUFFER.
Anger.
Clothes.

Cheats who ply in different parts of the town, particularly about Water-lane, opposite St. Clement's church, in the Strand, and pretend to deal in smuggled goods, stopping all country people, or such as they think they can impose on; which they frequently do, by selling them Spital-fields goods at double their current price.
A queer unaccountable fellow.
A tall, awkward, ill-made fellow.
A stupid, sluggish fellow, one long going on an errand.

Down in the dumps; low-spirited, melancholy: jocularly said to be derived from Dumpos, a king of Egypt, who died of melancholy. Dumps are also small pieces of lead, cast by schoolboys in the shape of money.
A stealer of cows and calves.
A privy. A water closet.
To open a door: a contraction of DO OPE or OPEN. See DUB.
Money. Down with your dust; deposit the money. To raise or kick up a dust; to make a disturbance or riot: see BREEZE. Dust it away; drink about.
A dead man: your father is a dustman.

To die hard, is to shew no signs of fear or contrition at the gallows; not to whiddle or squeak. This advice is frequently given to felons going to suffer the law, by their old comrades, anxious for the honour of the gang.
A deposit in part of payment, to bind a bargain.
A Grave.
Make the cull easy or quiet; gag or kill him. As easy as pissing the bed.
To eat like a beggar man, and wag his under jaw; a jocular reproach to a proud man. To eat one's words; to retract what one has said.
To excite, stimulate, or provoke; or as it is vulgarly called, to egg a man on. Fall back, fall edge; i.e. let what will happen. Some derive to egg on, from the Latin word, AGE, AGE.
Labour. Elbow grease will make an oak table shine.
Sufficient space to act in. Out at elbows; said of an estate that is mortgaged.
A gamester, one who rattles Saint Hugh's bones, i.e. the dice.
The King's Bench Prison. Lord Ellenborough's teeth; the chevaux de frize round the top of the wall of that prison.
Drunk as an emperor, i.e. ten times as drunk as a lord.
Porter.
A drunken man, who looks red in the face, or hoists his colours in his drink.
Rich; also, having new clothes. Well equipt; full of money, or well dressed. The cull equipped me with a brace of meggs; the gentleman furnished me with. a couple of guineas.
Hen roosts.
One that lurks about to rob hen-roosts; also a listener at doors and windows, to hear private conversation.
Washing day.
Killed: alluding to the gunner's accounts, wherein the articles consumed are charged under the title of expended. Sea phrase.
It's all my eye and Betty Martin. It's all nonsense, all mere stuff.
A bumper, a glass filled so full as to leave no room for the lip. Also a violent blow on the face.
It won't fadge; it won't do. A farthing.
One of the faithful; a taylor who gives long credit. His faith has made him unwhole; i.e. trusting too much, broke him.
A set of subterraneous rooms in the Fleet Prison.
A counterfeit signature. A forgery. Tell the macers to mind their fakements; desire the swindlers to be careful not to forge another person's signature.

entries.word: FALLEN AWAY FROM A HORSE LOAD TO A CART LOAD
entries.text: A saying on one grown fat.
A thief or receiver of stolen goods.
Going into a goldsmith's shop, under pretence of buying a wedding ring, and palming one or two, by daubing the hand with some viscous matter.
Hands. Famble cheats; rings or gloves. CANT.
To shake bands: figuratively, to agree or make up a difference. Famgrasp the cove; shake hands with the fellow. CANT.
To beat any one. I fanned him sweetly; I beat him heartily.
with more rags than ribands.

He has let a brewer's fart, grains and all; said of one who has bewrayed his breeches. Piss and fart. Sound at heart. Mingere cum bumbis, Res saluberrima est lumbis. I dare not trust my a-se with a fart: said by a person troubled with a looseness.
Breeches.
Excrement hanging about the anus.
A warrant.
Bogs.

The last landed, inned, or stowed, of any sort of merchandise: so called by the water-side porters, carmen, &c. All the fat is in the fire; that is, it is all over with us: a saying used in case of any miscarriage or disappointment in an undertaking; an allusion to overturning the frying pan into the fire. Fat, among printers, means void spaces.

entries.word: AS FAT AS A HEN IN THE FOREHEAD
entries.text: A saying of a meagre person.
A rich fellow.
Stupid.
A tumbler, juggler, or shewer of tricks; perhaps because they lure the people, as a faulconer does his hawks. CANT.
Fortune tellers.

A common fraud, thus practised: A fellow drops a brass ring, double gilt, which he picks up before the party meant to be cheated, and to whom he disposes of it for less than its supposed, and ten times more than its real, value. See MONEY DROPPER.
A ring.
The fundament.
To enrich one's self.
A rough or stony lane.
FAW, FUM. Nonsensical words, supposed in childish story-books to be spoken by giants. I am not to be frighted by fee, faw, fum; I am not to be scared by nonsense.
A spoon. To nab the feeder; to steal a spoon.
A sham attack on one part, when a real one is meant at another.

An empty bottle: so called at the university of Cambridge, where fellow commoners are not in general considered as over full of learning. At Oxford an empty bottle is called a gentleman commoner for the same reason. They pay at Cambridge 250 l. a year for the privilege of wearing a gold or silver tassel to their caps. The younger branches of the nobility have the privilege of wearing a hat, and from thence are denominated HAT FELLOW COMMONERS.

To pawn or sell to a receiver of stolen goods. The kiddey fenced his thimble for three quids; the young fellow pawned his watch for three guineas. To fence invariably means to pawn or sell goods to a receiver.
The magazine, or warehouse, where stolen goods are secreted.
A hole. CANT.
All those who have not the sham sores or clymes.

Andrea Ferrara; the name of a famous sword-cutler: most of the Highland broad-swords are marked with his name; whence an Andrea Ferrara has become the common name for the glaymore or Highland broad-sword. See CLAYMORE.

A tradesman who sells goods to young unthrift heirs, at excessive rates, and then continually duns them for the debt. To ferret; to search out or expel any one from his hiding-place, as a ferret drives out rabbits; also to cheat. Ferret-eyed; red-eyed: ferrets have red eyes.
A trick, wheedle, or invention to deceive.
To beat. Fib the cove's quarron in the rumpad for the lour in his bung; beat the fellow in the highway for the money in his purse. CANT.--A fib is also a tiny lie.
A quid, from the small pieces of tow with which the vent or touch hole of a cannon is stopped. SEA TERM.
Trifling discourse, nonsense. A mere fiddle faddle fellow; a trifier.
Nothing; the end of the ancient fiddlesticks ending in a point; hence metaphorically used to express a thing terminating in nothing.
He has got the fidgets; said of one that cannot sit long in a place.
General thieves; called also St. Peter's sons, having every finger a fish-hook. CANT.
All sixpences: sixpence being the usual sum paid by each couple, for music at country wakes and hops. Fiddler's fare; meat, drink, and money. Fiddler's pay; thanks and wine.
A baked sheep's head.
A red-faced man is said to have been served with a writ of fieri facias.
To kill.
One who alters figures on bank notes, converting tens to hundreds.
Fine as five pence. Fine as a cow-t--d stuck with primroses.
A man imprisoned for any offence. A fine of eighty-four months; a transportation for seven years.

A parson: so called, because he points out a way to others which he never goes himself. Like the finger post, he points out a way he has never been, and probably will never go, i.e. the way to heaven.

Introducing a story by head and shoulders. A man wanting to tell a particular story, said to the company, Hark! did you not hear a gun?--but now we are talking of a gun, I will tell you the story of one.
To drink a dram.
Villains who rob at fires under pretence of assisting in removing the goods.
A seaman. A scaly fish; a rough, blunt tar. To have other fish to fry; to have other matters to mind, something else to do.
Suitable. It won't fit; It will not suit or do.
The sign of five shillings, i.e. the crown. Fifteen shillings; the sign of the three crowns.
An escape backward,
Confounded.
Relaxed, flaccid, not firm or solid.
A groat. CANT.--The flag of defiance, or bloody flag is out; signifying the man is drunk, and alluding to the redness of his face. SEA PHRASE.
A lie, or sham story: also a single stroke on a drum. To flam; to hum, to amuse, to deceive. Flim flams; idle stories.
To blaze, shine or glare.
A periwig. Rum flash; a fine long wig. Queer flash; a miserable weather-beaten caxon.
To shew ostentatiously. To flash one's ivory; to laugh and shew one's teeth. Don't flash your ivory, but shut your potatoe trap, and keep your guts warm; the Devil loves hot tripes.
To vomit. CANT.
A house that harbours thieves.
The canting or slang language.
A bubble, gull, or silly fellow.
Drunk.
THE FOX. To vomit.
A trifling injury. To send any one away with a flea in his ear; to give any one a hearty scolding.
To rob, cheat, or plunder.
A drinking glass. CANT.
Grinning or laughing in a man's face.
Cutting. Flick me some panam and caffan; cut me some bread and cheese. Flick the peter; cut off the cloak-bag, or portmanteau.
To trick or cheat. He flung me fairly out of it: he cheated me out of it.
Journeymen taylors, who on a late occasion refused to work for the wages settled by law. Those who submitted, were by the mutineers styled dungs, i.e. dunghills.

Small beer, brandy, and sugar: this mixture, with the addition of a lemon, was by sailors, formerly called Sir Cloudsly, in memory of Sir Cloudsly Shovel, who used frequently to regale himself with it.
See CAMPBELL'S ACADEMY.
The hulks.
To whip.
A horsewhip. CANT.
To knock down. Floor the pig; knock down the officer.
To jeer, to ridicule.
Oatmeal and water boiled to a jelly; also compliments, neither of which are over-nourishing.
Drunk.
The recorder of a corporation; a recorder was an antient musical instrument.
To cheat, cozen, or over-reach; also to salivate. To flux a wig; to put it up in curl, and bake it.
Knowing. Acquainted with another's meaning or proceeding. The rattling cove is fly; the coachman knows what we are about.
A waggon. CANT.
Life-guard men, from their sitting on horseback, under an arch, where they are frequently observed to drive away flies with their swords.
Shoes.
Beggars plying in a body at funerals.
Turnpike gates.
A lock in wrestling, by which he who uses it throws his adversary over his head.
Sirreverence wrapped in paper and thrown over a neighbour's wall.

Cheats who obtain money by pretending to persons who have been lately robbed, that they may come from a place or party where, and from whom, they may receive information respecting the goods stolen from them, and demand payment as porters.
Ballad-singers and hawkers of penny histories.
A bank note.
Smoke. CANT.
A silk handkerchief,
An old fogram; a fusty old fellow.
Tobacco. Tip me a gage of fogus; give me a pipe of tobacco. CANT.
A fool at the end of a stick; a fool at one end, and a maggot at the other; gibes on an angler.
A bailiff.
Rogues who rob on foot.
A contemptuous appellation for a foot soldier, commonly used by the cavalry.
An artificial sore made with unslaked lime, soap, and the rust of old iron, on the back of a beggar's hand, as if hurt by the bite or kick of a horse.
Give us your fore foot; give us your hand.
One who engrosses all the talk to himself, or speaks for the rest of the company.
A gamester's last stake.
A judge, who tells every prisoner his fortune, lot or doom. To go before the fortune teller, lambskin men, or conjuror; to be tried at an assize. See LAMBSKIN MEN.
To foul a plate with a man, to take a dinner with him.
Abusive.

The name of a public house, where the Eccentrics assemble in May's Buildings, St. Martin's Lane. Fox. A sharp, cunning fellow. Also an old term for a sword, probably a rusty one, or else from its being dyed red with blood; some say this name alluded to certain swords of remarkable good temper, or metal, marked with the figure of a fox, probably the sign, or rebus, of the maker.
Intoxicated.
Rank. Stinking.
Mending the foot by capping it.
A pickpocket, cheat, or rogue. See WOTTON'S GANG.
Words or passages surreptitiously interpolated or inserted into a book or writing.
Vagabonds who beg with sham patents, or briefs, for hospitals, fires, inundations, &c.
Lawless robbers and plunderers: originally soldiers who served without pay, for the privilege of plundering the enemy.
Free of expence. To lush at Freeman's Quay; to drink at another's cost.
A thin, small, hard cider, much used by vintners and coopers in parting their wines, to lower the price of them, and to advance their gain. A freezing vintner; a vintner who balderdashes his wine.
Cambridge new comers to the university.

A dismal countenance. Before, and even long after the Reformation, Friday was a day of abstinence, or jour maigre. Immediately after the restoration of king Charles II. a proclamation was issued, prohibiting all publicans from dressing any suppers on a Friday.
To dance the Paddington frisk; to be hanged.
Used by thieves to signify searching a person whom they have robbed. Blast his eyes! frisk him.
Choaked, strangled, suffocated, or hanged. CANT.
Drunk. This is rum fuddle; this is excellent tipple, or drink. Fuddle; drunk. Fuddle cap; a drunkard.
Nonsense.
Loaded dice are called high and lowmen, or high and low fulhams, by Ben Jonson and other writers of his time; either because they were made at Fulham, or from that place being the resort of sharpers.
Jocular term for empty.
A cheat, or trick. Do you think to fun me out of it? Do you think to cheat me?--Also the breech, perhaps from being the abbreviation of fundament. I'll kick your fun. CANT.
To use an unfair motion of the hand in plumping at taw. SCHOOLBOY'S TERM.

To smoke; figuratively, to smoke or stink through fear. I was in a cursed funk. To funk the cobler; a schoolboy's trick, performed with assafoettida and cotton, which are stuffed into a pipe: the cotton being lighted, and the bowl of the pipe covered with a coarse handkerchief, the smoke is blown out at the small end, through the crannies of a cobler's stall.
Aldermen.
Wheat boiled up to a jelly. To simper like a furmity kettle: to smile, or look merry about the gills.
A confusion, a hurry, an unnecessary to do about trifles.
