Bombast language. Red fustian; port wine.
To shuffle cards minutely: also, to change the pack.
The mouth. Gift of the gab; a facility of speech, nimble tongued eloquence. To blow the gab; to confess, or peach.
STRING. A bridle.
A foolish fellow.
A fair. The drop coves maced the joskins at the gaff; the ring-droppers cheated the countryman at the fair.
To game by tossing up halfpence.
An instrument used chiefly by housebreakers and thieves, for propping open the mouth of a person robbed, thereby to prevent his calling out for assistance.
A quart pot, or a pint; also a pipe. CANT.
A pipe of tobacco.
High and Low. Cheats, who by sham pretences, and wonderful stories of their sufferings, impose on the credulity of well meaning people. See RUM GAGGER.
A hodgepodge made up of the remnants and scraps of the larder.
His gall is not yet broken; a saying used in prisons of a man just brought in, who appears dejected.

Building the galley; a game formerly used at sea, in order to put a trick upon a landsman, or fresh-water sailor. It being agreed to play at that game, one sailor personates the builder, and another the merchant or contractor: the builder first begins by laying the keel, which consists of a number of men laid all along on their backs, one after another, that is, head to foot; he next puts in the ribs or knees, by making a number of men sit feet to feet, at right angles to, and on each side of, the keel: he now fixing on the person intended to be the object of the joke, observes he is a fierce-looking fellow, and fit for the lion; he accordingly places him at the head, his arms being held or locked in by the two persons next to him, representing the ribs. After several other dispositions, the builder delivers over the galley to the contractor as complete: but he, among other faults and objections, observes the lion is not gilt, on which the builder or one of his assistants, runs to the head, and dipping a mop in the excrement, thrusts it into the face of the lion.
A city barge, used formerly on the lord mayor's day, when he was sworn in at Westminster.
Breeches.
A nick namefor an apothecary,
Plenty.
A grief, or pickpocket; also one that associates with them.
Leathern cases of stiff leather, used in Devonshire instead of boots; they are fastened to the saddle, and admit the leg, shoe and all: the name was at first jocularly given.
A sharper, of tricking, gamester.
To humbug. To deceive, To tell lies. What rum gamon the old file pitched to the flat; how finely the knowing old fellow humbugged the fool.
Common place talk of any profession; as the gamon and patter of a horse-dealer, sailor, &c.
The mouth or lips. Cant.
A company of men, a body of sailors, a knot of thieves, pickpockets, &c. A gang of sheep trotters; the four feet of a sheep.
A hurdle: traitors being usually conveyed from the gaol, to the place of execution, on a hurdle or sledge.
Sights; any thing to feed the eye. I am come abroad for a little gapeseed.
An entrance fee demanded by the old prisoners of one just committed to gaol.
The head. His garret, or upper story, is empty, or unfurnished; i.e. he has no brains, he is a fool.
An elevated observatory or summer-house.
It won't gee; it won't hit or do, it does not suit or fit.
The art of shoemaking. One of the gentle craft: a shoemaker: so called because once practised by St. Crispin.
An empty bottle; an university joke, gentlemen commoners not being deemed over full of learning.
A louse.
A highway robber, because he makes a gentleman obey his commands, i.e. stand and deliver.
In debt, in gaol, and in danger of remaining there for life: or, in gaol, indicted, and in danger of being hanged in chains.
That is, without money, without wit, and without manners: some add another out, i.e. without credit.
A gentleman. CANT.
A gentleman's house. CANT.
One of his get; one of his offspring, or begetting.
A horse that shrinks from the collar and will not draw.
A two-legged stool, used to support the body of a coach whilst finishing.
Small white specks under the finger nails, said to portend gifts or presents. A stingy man is said to be as full of gifts as a brazen horse of his farts.
A facility of speech.
A latch, or door. Dub the gigger; open the door. Gigger dubber; the turnkey of a jaol.
The cheeks. To look rosy about the gills; to have a fresh complexion. To look merry about the gills: to appear cheerful.

A thief who picks locks, so called from the gilt or picklock key: many of them are so expert, that, from the lock of a church door to that of the smallest cabinet, they will find means to open it; these go into reputable public houses, where, pretending business, they contrive to get into private rooms, up stairs, where they open any bureaus or trunks they happen to find there.
A distiller.
A cake made of treacle, flour, and grated ginger; also money. He has the gingerbread; he is rich.

Gilding and carving: these terms are particularly applied by seamen on board Newcastle colliers, to the decorations of the sterns and quarters of West-Indiamen, which they have the greatest joy in defacing.
Softly, gently, tenderly. To go gingerly to work: to attempt a thing gently, or cautiously.
An instrument to lift up a great, in order to steal what is in the window. CANT. GIP from gups a WOLF. A servant at college.
Quips, taunts, severe or biting reflections.
To grumble in the gizzard; to be secretly displeased.
A Highland broad-sword; from the Erse GLAY, or GLAIVE, a sword; and MORE, great.
A window.

One who breaks windows and shew-glasses, to steal goods exposed for sale. Glaziers; eyes. CANT.--Is your father a glazier; a question asked of a lad or young man, who stands between the speaker and the candle, or fire. If it is answered in the negative, the rejoinder is--I wish he was, that he might make a window through your body, to enable us to see the fire or light.
Smooth, slippery. Glib tongued; talkative.
A candle, or dark lantern, used in housebreaking; also fire. To glim; to burn in the hand. CANT.
Andirons. CANT.
Angry, or in a passion. CANT.
A link-boy. CANT.
Fire. CANT.
Persons begging with sham licences, pretending losses by fire.
Eyes.
A candlestick. CANT.
Pewter. CANT.
Sullen.
A term used by bruisers to signify a man who will bear a great deal of beating.
A little dog that by his barking alarms the family when any person is breaking into the house.
THE. The dash. The mode. He is quite the go, he is quite varment, he is prime, he is bang up, are synonimous expressions.
A writing. CANT.

The Queen's Head in Duke's court, Bow street, Covent Garden; frequented by the under players: where gin and water was sold in three-halfpenny bowls, called Goes; the gin was called Arrack. The go, the fashion; as, large hats are all the go.
Those who wheedle in chapmen for horse-dealers.
The mouth; also a bit or morsel: whence gobbets. Gift of the gob; wide-mouthed, or one who speaks fluently, or sings well.
A bridle.

He who pays the reckoning, or answers for the rest of the company: as, Will you stand godfather, and we will take care of the brat; i.e. repay you another time. Jurymen are also called godfathers, because they name the crime the prisoner before them has been guilty of, whether felony, petit larceny, &c.
All-a-gog; impatient, anxious, or desirous of a thing.

Two giants, whose effigies stand on each side of the clock in Guildhall, London; of whom there is a tradition, that, when they hear the clock strike one, on the first of April, they will walk down from their places.
Eyes: see OGLES. Goggle eyes; large prominent eyes. To goggle; to stare.
Going out to break open, or pick the locks of, houses.

Sharpers who drop a piece of gold, which they pick up in the presence of some unexperienced person, for whom the trap is laid, this they pretend to have found, and, as he saw them pick it up, they invite him to a public house to partake of it: when there, two or three of their comrades drop in, as if by accident, and propose cards, or some other game, when they seldom fail of stripping their prey.
One whose employment is to empty necessary houses; called also a tom-turd-man, and night-man: the latter, from that business being always performed in the night.
One who has commonly a purse full of gold. Goldfinches; guineas.

entries.word: GOLGOTHA OR THE PLACE OF SCULLS
entries.text: Part of the Theatre at Oxford, where the heads of houses sit; those gentlemen being by the wits of the university called sculls.
A large, clumsy fellow.
i.e. Goliah's shoes. Large leathern clogs, worn by invalids over their ordinary shoes.
Like Goodyer's pig; never well but when in mischief.

A taylor's goose; a smoothing iron used to press down the seams, for which purpose it must be heated: hence it is a jocular saying, that a taylor, be he ever so poor, is always sure to have a goose at his fire. He cannot say boh to a goose; a saying of a bashful or sheepish fellow.

A goose, whose neck is greased, being suspended by the legs to a cord tied to two trees or high posts, a number of men on horseback, riding full speed, attempt to pull off the head: which if they effect, the goose is their prize. This has been practised in Derbyshire within the memory of persons now living.
He played up old gooseberry among them; said of a person who, by force or threats, suddenly puts an end to a riot or disturbance.
A large frizzled wig: perhaps from a supposed likeness to a gooseberry bush.
A church.
Money, chiefly gold: perhaps from the traffic carried on at that place, which is chiefly for gold dust. CANT.
To seize. To grabble the bit; to seize any one's money. CANT.
To seize a man. The pigs grabbed the kiddey for a crack: the officers, seized the youth for a burglary.
Corn.
Hoarded money: supposed to have belonged to the grandmother of the possessor.
Handcuffs.
Like a grave digger; up to the a-se in business, and don't know which way to turn.
As great as shirt and shitten a-se.
A surtout. CANT.
A covetous or voracious person.
St. Giles's Greek; the slang lingo, cant, or gibberish.
Doctor Green; i.e. grass: a physician, or rather medicine, found very successful in curing most disorders to which horses are liable. My horse is not well, I shall send him to Doctor Green.

Young, inexperienced, unacquainted; ignorant. How green the cull was not to stag how the old file planted the books. How ignorant the booby was not to perceive how the old sharper placed the cards in such a manner as to insure the game.

An attorney: those gentlemen carry their clients' deeds in a green bag; and, it is said, when they have no deeds to carry, frequently fill them with an old pair of breeches, or any other trumpery, to give themselves the appearance of business.
An inexperienced young man.
Retailers of sand from the pits at and about Greenwich, in Kent: perhaps they are styled barbers, from their constant shaving the sandbanks.
A pensioner of Greenwich Hospital.
The gallows: so named from Gregory Brandon, a famous finisher of the law; to whom Sir William Segar, garter king of arms (being imposed on by Brooke, a herald), granted a coat of arms.
A farmer who rents the tithes of the rector or vicar.
A farthing. A merry grig; a fellow as merry as a grig: an allusion to the apparent liveliness of a grig, or young eel.
Old Mr. Grim; death.
To grin in a glass case; to be anatomized for murder: the skeletons of many criminals are preserved in glass cases, at Surgeons' hall.
THE CAT'S UNCLE. A foolish grinning fellow, one who grins without reason.
Teeth. Gooseberry grinder; the breech. Ask bogey, the gooseberry grinder; ask mine a-se.

To save his groats; to come off handsomely: at the universities, nine groats are deposited in the hands of an academic officer, by every person standing for a degree; which if the depositor obtains with honour, the groats are returned to him.

Rum and water. Grog was first introduced into the navy about the year 1740, by Admiral Vernon, to prevent the sailors intoxicating themselves with their allowance of rum, or spirits. Groggy, or groggified; drunk.
A grogged horse; a foundered horse.
A horse. CANT.
A grave.
A hog, or pig. SEA TERM.
Victuals. To grub; to dine.

A street near Moorfields, formerly the supposed habitation of many persons who wrote for the booksellers: hence a Grub-street writer means a hackney author, who manufactures booss for the booksellers.
Lying intelligence.
To make foul or dirty.
To grumble in the gizzard; to murmur or repine. He grumbled like a bear with a sore head.
A discontented person; one who is always railing at the times or ministry.
A hog; to grunt; to groan, or complain of sickness.
A smoaked hog's face.
Pork, bacon, or any kind of hog's flesh.
Tea.
One easily imposed on. To gudgeon; to swallow the bait, or fall into a trap: from the fish of that name, which is easily taken.
A simple credulous fellow, easily cheated.
Deceived, cheated, imposed on.
Usurers who lend money to the gamesters.
Abusive language. Come, let us have no more of your gum.
Docility, comprehension, capacity.
He is in the gun; he is drunk: perhaps from an allusion to a vessel called a gun, used for ale in the universities.
My great guts are ready to eat my little ones; my guts begin to think my throat's cut; my guts curse my teeth: all expressions signifying the party is extremely hungry.
Exceeding hungry.
or TORMENTOR of CATGUT. A fiddler.
The throat, the swallow, the red lane. See RED LANE.
Taking out the lining of it: i. e. drinking it off. Gutting an oyster; eating it. Gutting a house; clearing it of its furniture. See POULTERER.
A dark lanthorn: an allusion to Guy Faux, the principal actor in the gunpowder plot. Stow the guy: conceal the lanthorn.
Liquor. To guzzle; to drink greedily.
One greedy of liquor.
Any writing or pass with a seal.
Jeering or ridiculing.
A college runner or errand-boy at Cambridge, called at Oxford a scout. See SCOUT.
A schoolmaster, or usher.
One who writes for attornies or booksellers.
Captain Hackum; a bravo, a slasher.

A weapon carried by a serjeant of foot. To get a halbert; to be appointed a serjeant. To be brought to the halberts; to be flogged a la militaire: soldiers of the infantry, when flogged, being commonly tied to three halberts, set up in a triangle, with a fourth fastened across them. He carries the halbert in his face; a saying of one promoted from a serjeant to a commission officer.
Sixpence.
Almost drunk.
A high constable. Cant.
or HAMCASES Breeches.
A sailor. We lost a hand; we lost a sailor. Bear a hand; make haste. Hand to fist; opposite: the same as tete-a-tete, or cheek by joul.
To know how to handle one's fists; to be skilful in the art of boxing. The cove flashes a rare handle to his physog; the fellow has a large nose.
This, in advertisements, means a horse-whipping.
To hang back, to hesitate.
A thievish, or villainous appearance.

A vile, desperate fellow. Persons guilty of murder, or other atrocious crimes, are frequently, after execution, hanged on a gibbet, to which they are fastened by iron bandages; the gibbet is commonly placed on or near the place where the crime was committed.
Score it up: speaking of a reckoning.
The traps scavey where we hang out; the officers know where we live.
A dependant.
He has a hank on him; i.e. an ascendancy over him, or a hold upon him. A Smithfield hank; an ox, rendered furious by overdriving and barbarous treatment. See BULL HANK.
To hanker after any thing; to have a longing after or for it.
Stale beer, nearly sour, is said to be hard. Hard also means severe: as, hard fate, a hard master.
Close after him.
He has swallowed a hare; he is drunk; more probably a HAIR, which requires washing down,
Whispering on one side to borrow money.
A constable. CANT.
A beadle. CANT.
The stocks. CANT.
A country fellow. CANT.--Old Harry; the Devil.
He was running harum scarum; said of any one running or walking hastily, and in a hurry, after they know not what.
To flash the hash; to vomit. CANT.
Precipitate, passionate. He is none of the Hastings sort; a saying of a slow, loitering fellow: an allusion to the Hastings pea, which is the first in season.

Oatmeal and milk boiled to a moderate thickness, and eaten with sugar and butter. Figuratively, a wet, muddy road: as, The way through Wandsworth is quite a hasty pudding. To eat hot hasty pudding for a laced hat, or some other prize, is a common feat at wakes and fairs.
Under the hatches; in trouble, distress, or debt.
A sheep. CANT.
Wavering, doubtful, shilly shally.
Ware hawk; the word to look sharp, a bye-word when a bailiff passes. Hawk also signifies a sharper, in opposition to pigeon. See PIGEON. See WARE HAWK.

Licensed itinerant retailers of different commodities, called also pedlars; likewise the sellers of news-papers. Hawking; an effort to spit up the thick phlegm, called OYSTERS: whence it is wit upon record, to ask the person so doing whether he has a licence; a punning allusion to the Act of hawkers and pedlars.
To beat any one with a hazel stick.

entries.word: HEAD CULLY OF THE PASS, or PASSAGE BANK
entries.text: The top tilter of that gang throughout the whole army, who demands and receives contribution from all the pass banks in the camp.
Teeth. SEA PHRASE.
Ears. CANT.
Gin.
He will have a hearty choak and caper sauce for breakfast; i.e. he will be hanged.
To rob. To heave a case; to rob a house. To heave a bough; to rob a booth. CANT.
Thieves who make it their business to steal tradesmen's shop-books. CANT.
bully, a swaggering coward. To hector; to bully, probably from such persons affecting the valour of Hector, the Trojan hero.

To make a hedge; to secure a bet, or wager, laid on one side, by taking the odds on the other, so that, let what will happen, a certain gain is secured, or hedged in, by the person who takes this precaution; who is then said to be on velvet.
A small obscure alehouse.
A robber of hedges.
An illiterate unbeneficed curate, a patrico.

To he laid by the heels; to be confined, or put in prison. Out at heels; worn, or diminished: his estate or affairs are out at heels. To turn up his heels; to turn up the knave of trumps at the game of all-fours.
A peg in the heel of a shoe, taken out when it is finished. A person leaving any liquor in his glass, is frequently called upon by the toast-master to take off his heel-tap.
A taylor's repository for his stolen goods, called cabbage: see CABBAGE. Little hell; a small dark covered passage, leading from London-wall to Bell-alley.
A wicked abandoned fellow.
The Cambridge driver of the Telegraph. The favorite companion of the University fashionables, and the only tutor to whose precepts they attend.
To run helter skelter, hand over head, in defiance of order.
Young hemp; an appellation for a graceless boy.
A man who was hanged is said to have died of a hempen fever; and, in Dorsetshire, to have been stabbed with a Bridport dagger; Bridport being a place famous for manufacturing hemp into cords.
Cowardly.
One who has no settled place of residence.
The devil a barrel the better herring; all equally bad.
The sea. To cross the herring pond at the king's expence; to be transported.
Drinking twice to the same person.
A country hick; an ignorant clown. CANT.
Tipsey; quasi, hickupping.

A childish game. He plays at hide and seek; a saying of one who is in fear of being arrested for debt, or apprehended for some crime, and therefore does not chuse to appear in public, but secretly skulks up and down. See SKULK.
Stingy, hard of delivery; a poet poor in invention, is said to have a hidebound muse.
Confusedly mixed.
To eat skylarks in a garret.
Tories, Jacobites.
A gambler at dice, who, having a strong head, drinks to intoxicate his adversary, or pigeon.
A highwayman. CANT.
To be on the high ropes; to be in a passion.
A country clown.
It is high water, with him; he is full of money.
To hike off; to run away. CANT.
To kick out a hind leg; to make a rustic bow.
MY HONEY. A north country hinney, particularly a Northumbrian: in that county, hinney is the general term of endearment.
Bantering, ridiculing. Hoaxing a quiz; joking an odd fellow. UNIVERSITY WIT.
a clown.

Will you hob or nob with me? a question formerly in fashion at polite tables, signifying a request or challenge to drink a glass of wine with the proposer: if the party challenged answered Nob, they were to chuse whether white or red. This foolish custom is said to have originated in the days of good queen Bess, thus: when great chimnies were in fashion, there was at each corner of the hearth, or grate, a small elevated projection, called the hob; and behind it a seat. In winter time the beer was placed on the hob to warm: and the cold beer was set on a small table, said to have been called the nob; so that the question, Will you have hob or nob? seems only to have meant, Will you have warm or cold beer? i.e. beer from the hob, or beer from the nob.
Half a man and half a boy, a lad between both.
Impeded, interrupted, puzzled. To hobble; to walk lamely.
A pace between a walk and a run, a dog-trot.
Sir Posthumous's hobby; one nice or whimsical in his clothes.
A man who is a great keeper or rider of hobby horses; one that is apt to be strongly attached to his systems of amusement.

That or none; from old Hobson, a famous carrier of Cambridge, who used to let horses to the students; but never permitted them to chuse, always allotting each man the horse he thought properest for his manner of riding and treatment.
vulgar appellation for the feet. You have left the marks of your dirty hocks on my clean stairs; a frequent complaint from a mop squeezer to a footman.
Drunk with strong stale beer, called old hock. See HICKEY.
Brother Hod; a familiar name for a bricklayer's labourer: from the hod which is used for carrying bricks and mortar.
An abbreviation of Roger: a general name for a country booby.
An irregular mixture of numerous things.
Snails in their shells.
A mean stingy fellow.
Rude, unmannerly, filthy.
Corruption of haut goust, high taste, or flavour; commonly said of flesh somewhat tainted. It has a confounded hogo; it stinks confoundedly.

To go upon the hoist; to get into windows accidentally left open: this is done by the assistance of a confederate, called the hoist, who leans his head against the wall, making his back a kind of step or ascent.

To ride backwards up Holborn hill; to go to the gallows: the way to Tyburn, the place of execution for criminals condemned in London, was up that hill. Criminals going to suffer, always ride backwards, as some conceive to increase the ignominy, but more probably to prevent them being shocked with a distant view of the gallows; as, in amputations, surgeons conceal the instruments with which they are going to operate. The last execution at Tyburn, and consequently of this procession, was in the year 1784, since which the criminals have been executed near Newgate
It was quiet a hollow thing; i.e. a certainty, or decided business.

The first month after marriage. A poor honey; a harmless, foolish, goodnatured fellow. It is all honey or a t--d with them; said of persons who are either in the extremity of friendship or enmity, either kissing or fighting.
Blindfolded by a handkerchief, or other ligature, bound over the eyes.
To beat the hoof; to travel on foot. He hoofed it or beat the hoof, every step of the way from Chester to London.

WITH NIX THE BUFFER. This rig consists in feeding a man and a dog for nothing, and is carried on thus: Three men, one of who pretends to be sick and unable to eat, go to a public house: the two well men make a bargain with the landlord for their dinner, and when he is out of sight, feed their pretended sick companion and dog gratis.
An expression signifying that the story is not true, or that the thing will not occour.
See ANGLERS.
To run away. CANT.
A dancing master. See CAPER MERCHANT.
To draw in one's horns; to retract an assertion through fear: metaphor borrowed from a snail, who on the apprehension of danger, draws in his horns, and retires to his shell.
A kiss with a loud smack; also a bite.
A meal without drinking.
Ale and brandy made hot.
He has so hot a stomach, that he burns all the clothes off his back; said of one who pawns his clothes to purchase liquor.
Confusedly. To fire hubble de shuff, to fire quick and irregularly. OLD MILITARY TERM.
A noise, riot, or disturbance.
Beer, egg, and brandy, made hot.
Itinerant retailers of provisions. He is in hucksters hands; he is in a bad way.
To lash. The cove was hued in the naskin; the rogue was soundly lashed in bridewell. CANT.
To hug brown bess; to carry a firelock, or serve as a private soldier. He hugs it as the Devil hugs a witch: said of one who holds any thing as if he was afraid of losing it.
By stealth, privately, without making an appearance. They spent their money in a hugger mugger way.
A society existing in 1748.
A great hulky fellow; an over-grown clumsy lout, or fellow.

To deceive, or impose on one by some story or device. A humbug; a jocular imposition, or deception. To hum and haw; to hesitate in speech, also to delay, or be with difficulty brought to consent to any matter or business,
Persons at church. There is a great number of hums in the autem; there is a great congregation in the church.
A pulpit.
Very old and strong beer, called also stingo. See STINGO.

A hum drum fellow; a dull tedious narrator, a bore; also a set of gentlemen, who (Bailey says) used to meet near the Charter House, or at the King's Head in St. John's-street, who had more of pleasantry, and less of mystery, than the free masons.
The brethren of the venerable society of humbugs was held at brother Hallam's, in Goodman's Fields.
A great lye, a rapper. See RAPPER.
Double ale, stout pharaoh. See PHARAOH.

A musical instrument made of a mopstick, a bladder, and some packthread, thence also called a bladder and string, and hurdy gurdy; it is played on like a violin, which is sometimes ludicrously called a humstrum; sometimes, instead of a bladder, a tin canister is used.
A covetous miserable fellow, a miser; also the name of a famous bear mentioned by Ben Jonson.
Drawing in unwary persons to play or game. CANT.
A kind of fiddle, originally made perhaps out of a gourd. See HUMSTRUM.
A rout, riot, bustle or confusion.
Hush the cull; murder the fellow.
Money given to hush up or conceal a robbery, theft, or any other offence, or to take off the evidence from appearing against a criminal.

Said to have been originally the cry of the huzzars or Hungarian light horse; but now the national shout of the English, both civil and military, in the sea phrase termed a cheer; to give three cheers being to huzza thrice.
The hypochondriac: low spirits. He is hypped; he has got the blue devils, &c.
A farthing, a small bowl serving as the mark for bowlers. An instrument for pulling off boots.
A fool. Jack Adams's parish; Clerkenwell.
A poor hackney parson.
An insolent fellow in authority.
The hangman; vide DERRICK and KETCH.
A sea term, signifying a common sailor.

A tall long-legged man; also a giant, said to be buried in Weston church, near Baldock, in Hertfordshire, where there are two stones fourteen feet distant, said to be the head and feet stones of his grave. This giant, says Salmon, as fame goes, lived in a wood here, and was a great robber, but a generous one; for he plundered the rich to feed the poor: he frequently took bread for this purpose from the Baldock bakers, who catching him at an advantage, put out his eyes, and afterwards hanged him upon a knoll in Baldock field. At his death he made one request, which was, that he might have his bow and arrow put into his hand, and on shooting it off, where the arrow fell, they would bury him; which being granted, the arrow fell in Weston churchyard. Above seventy years ago, a very large thigh bone was taken out of the church chest, where it had lain many years for a show, and was sold by the clerk to Sir John Tradescant, who, it is said, put it among the rarities of Oxford.
The merry andrew, zany, or jester to a mountebank.

Before one could say Jack Robinson; a saying to express a very short time, originating from a very volatile gentleman of that appellation, who would call on his neighbours, and be gone before his name could be announced.
A sailor.
An ape; a pert, ugly, little fellow.
Spavined. A jacked horse.
See JARKMEN.
Gin.
A soft fellow. A fool.
A ladder: perhaps from Jacob's dream. CANT. Also the common name for a jay, jays being usually taught to say, Poor Jacob! a cup of sack for Jacob.
A ditch: perhaps from jakes.
Prisoners.
A house of office, a cacatorium.
Hanged. CANT.
The mob, sometimes so called; also bailiffs, their setters, and followers.
Ordained. To be japanned; to enter into holy orders, to become a clergyman, to put on the black cloth: from the colour of the japan ware, which is black.
A seal.
Those, who fabricate counterfeit passes, licences, and certificates for beggars.
A hackney coachman.
A citizen cheated of his gold.
Speech, discourse. Give us none of your jaw; let us have none of your discourse. A jaw-me-dead; a talkative fellow. Jaw work; a cry used in fairs by the sellers of nuts.
A bob wig.
The knowledge box, the head. See KNOWLEDGE BOX.
It will be done in a jeffy; it will be done in a short space of time, in an instant.
To drive jehu-like; to drive furiously: from a king of Israel of that name, who was a famous charioteer, and mentioned as such in the Bible.
A gold ring. CANT.
A smart spruce fellow.
A crow. This instrument is much used by housebreakers. Sometimes called Jemmy Rook.
An instrument for lifting up the grate or top of a show-glass, in order to rob it. CANT.
To shake, towzle, or tumble about.
A smart jemmy fellow, a fopling.
A lawyer. Autem jet; a parson.

A method of deceiving seamen, by fixing a candle and lanthorn round the neck of a horse, one of whose fore feet is tied up; this at night has the appearance of a ship's light. Ships bearing towards it, run on shore, and being wrecked, are plundered by the inhabitants. This diabolical device is, it is said, practised by the inhabitants of our western coasts.
A whipping-post. CANT.
Leathern jacks tipped with silver, and hung with bells, formerly in use among fuddle caps. CANT.
A wild, thoughtless, rattling fellow.
Horse cosers, frequenting country fairs.
Usurers who attend the gaming-tables, and lend money at great premiums.
Cutting out the backs of coaches, and robbing the seats.
Encroaching.
Black Indies; Newcastle.
A silk handkerchief.
Breeches.
Supposed to be a very brotherly set of people; 'as great as two inkle weavers' being a proverbial saying.
Well inlaid; in easy circumstances, rich or well to pass.
Reproof instead of consolation.
One who brings news of some additional misfortune.
A reproof.
The head.
To reprove or reprehend. CAMBRIDGE TERM.
Any robbery. To do a job; to commit some kind of robbery.
To keep on a jogg-trot; to get on with a slow but regular pace.
The head. I'll lump your jolly nob for you; I'll give you a knock on the head.
A merry facetious fellow; a BON VIVANT, who never flinches from his glass, nor cries to go home to bed.
A large head; metaphorically a stupid fellow.
A great blow, or staff. I'll tip him a jordain if I transnear; i.e. I'll give him a blow with my staff, if I come near him. CANT.
A chamber-pot.
A jugg, or large pitcher.
A countryman. The dropcove maced the Joskin of twenty quid; The ring dropper cheated the countryman of twenty guineas.
To keep an ironmonger's shop by the side of a common, where the sheriff sets one up; to be hanged in chains. Iron-bound; laced. An iron-bound hat; a silver-laced hat.
He drank out of the bottle till he saw the island; the island is the rising bottom of a wine bottle, which appears like an island in the centre, before the bottle is quite empty.
Teeth. How the swell flashed his ivories; how the gentleman shewed his teeth.
See DOUBLE JUG.
The engine for burning culprits in the hand. CANT.
A licence.
A rough road or lane.

The jump, or dining-room jump; a species of robbery effected by ascending a ladder placed by a sham lamp-lighter, against the house intended to be robbed. It is so called, because, should the lamp-lighter be put to flight, the thief who ascended the ladder has no means of escaping but that of jumping down.
A round scolding bout.
A JOURNIERE mast; i.e. a mast for the day or occasion.
A punning appellation for a justice.
A picklock. 'Tis a rum kate; it is a clever picklock. CANT.
Men employed to load and unload the coal vessels.
Condition, order. Out of kelter; out of order.
Money.

William Kemp, said to have been the original Dogberry in Much ado about Nothing, danced a morris from London to Norwich in nine days: of which he printed the account, A. D. 1600, intitled, Kemp's Nine Days Wonder, &c.

Would I had Kemp's shoes to throw after you. BEN JONSON. Perhaps Kemp was a man remarkable for his good luck or fortune; throwing an old shoe, or shoes, after any one going on an important business, being by the vulgar deemed lucky.
A house. A bob ken, or a bowman ken; a well-furnished house, also a house that harbours thieves. Biting the ken; robbing the house. CANT.
A housebreaker. CANT.
To take away the street door: a method practised by the landlords in Kent-street, Southwark, when their tenants are above a fortnight's rent in arrear.
When a person has perplexed his affairs in general, or any particular business, he is said to have made a fine kettle of fish of it.

Breeches. A high kick; the top of the fashion. It is all the kick; it is the present mode. Tip us your kicks, we'll have them as well as your lour; pull off your breeches, for we must have them as well as your money. A kick; sixpence. Two and a kick; half-a-crown. A kick in the guts; a dram of gin, or any other spirituous liquor. A kick up; a disturbance, also a hop or dance. An odd kick in one's gallop; a strange whim or peculiarity.
To die. He kicked the bucket one day: he died one day. To kick the clouds before the hotel door; i.e. to be hanged.
Breeches.

To coax or wheedle. To inveigle. To amuse a man or divert his attention while another robs him. The sneaksman kidded the cove of the ken, while his pall frisked the panney; the thief amused the master of the house, while his companion robbed the house.

Rogues who make it their business to defraud young apprentices, or errand-boys, of goods committed to their charge, by prevailing on them to execute some trifling message, pretending to take care of their parcels till they come back; these are, in cant terms, said to be on the kid lay.
A forestaller: see CROCKER. Kidders are also persons employed by the gardeners to gather peas.
Young thieves.
Disposition, principles, humour. Of a strange kidney; of an odd or unaccountable humour. A man of a different kidney; a man of different principles.
New still-burnt rum.
Port wine.
Fetters.
One of the king's bad bargains; a malingeror, or soldier who shirks his duty.

entries.word: KING'S HEAD INN, or CHEQUER INN
entries.text: IN NEWGATE STREET. The prison of Newgate.
Coin, money.
He is gone to kingdom come, he is dead.
The skin of a large calf, in the language of the Excise-office.
An offer, as Fielding observes, very frequently made, but never, as he could learn, literally accepted. A kiss mine a-se fellow; a sycophant.
That part where the loaves have touched the oven.

A dancing-master, so called from his kit or cittern, a small fiddle, which dancing-masters always carry about with them, to play to their scholars. The kit is likewise the whole of a soldier's necessaries, the contents of his knapsack: and is used also to express the whole of different commodities: as, Here, take the whole kit; i.e. take all.
Food, good meat roasted or boiled. A little kitchen physic will set him up; he has more need of a cook than a doctor.

A jocular method of hobbling or bothering a troublesome teller of long stories: this is done by contradicting some very immaterial circumstance at the beginning of the narration, the objections to which being settled, others are immediately started to some new particular of like consequence; thus impeding, or rather not suffering him to enter into, the main story. Kittle pitchering is often practised in confederacy, one relieving the other, by which the design is rendered less obvious.
Effects, furniture; stock in trade. To seize one's kittys; to take his sticks.
A toy-shop, a nick-nack-atory.
A sheep's head. CANT.

A knave of the first rate: a phrase borrowed from the dyehouse, where certain colours are said to be in grain, to denote their superiority, as being dyed with cochineal, called grain. Knave in grain is likewise a pun applied to a cornfactor or miller.
A bully.
A false evidence, one that is ready to swear any thing for hire.
A footman: from the variety of colours in the liveries and trimming of gentlemen of that cloth.
A highwayman.
A taylor.

entries.word: KNIGHT OF THE THIMBLE, or NEEDLE
entries.text: A taylor or stay-maker.
A coachman.
A great eater.
more hog than gentleman. A saying of any low pretender to precedency.
The head. See NOB.
Strong ale or beer, stingo.
A crew, gang, or fraternity. He has tied a knot with his tongue, that he cannot untie with his teeth: i.e. he is married.

Sportsmen on the turf, who from experience and an acquaintance with the jockies, are supposed to be in the secret, that is, to know the true merits or powers of each horse; notwithstanding which it often happens that the knowing ones are taken in.
The head.
To steal his handkerchief.
Ruffles.
Stealing large pieces of coal from coalsheds.
Beating. I'll lace your jacket handsomely.
To go up the ladder to rest; to be hanged.
A man transported. The cove was lagged for a drag. The man was transported for stealing something out of a waggon.
A term of ridicule applied to men who being under sentence of transportation, pretend illness, to avoid being sent from gaol to the hulks.
To drop behind, to keep back. Lag last; the last of a company.
Water. CANT.
A buck of linen.

entries.word: LAID ON THE SHELF, or LAID UP IN LAVENDER
entries.text: Pawned.
To beat. Lamb pye; a beating: from lambo.
Apples roasted and put into strong ale.
The judges: from their robes lined and bordered with ermine.
How lies the land? How stands the reckoning? Who has any land in Appleby? a question asked the man at whose door the glass stands long, or who does not circulate it in due time.
Vagabonds lurking about the country who subsist by pilfering.
Highwaymen.
Butter-milk or whey. CANT.
A boat.
A piece of merriment. People playing together jocosely.
Blacking: Larry Dugan was a famous shoe-black at Dublin.
Let in.
A nick-name for an attorney; from the name of a writ.
Laid up in lavender; pawned.
To laugh on the wrong side of the mouth; to cry. I'll make him laugh on the wrong (or t'other) side of his mouth.

To give law to a hare; a sporting term, signifying to give the animal a chance of escaping, by not setting on the dogs till the hare is at some distance; it is also more figuratively used for giving any one a chance of succeeding in a scheme or project.
Enterprize, pursuit, or attempt: to be sick of the lay. It also means a hazard or chance: he stands a queer lay; i.e. he is in danger. CANT.
A dunghill about London, on which the soil brought from necessary houses is emptied; or, in more technical terms, where the old gold collected at weddings by the Tom t--d man, is stored.
Lazy people frequently take up more than they can safely carry, to save the trouble of coming a second time.
An instrument like a pair of tongs, for old or very fat people to take any thing from the ground without stooping.
To make water.
Apt to blab; one who cannot keep a secret is said to be leaky.
To play least in sight; to hide, keep out of the way, or make one's self scarce.
On one's guard. See PEERY.
Sham leggers; cheats who pretend to sell smuggled goods, but in reality only deal in old shop-keepers or damaged goods.
Spare diet.
A priest or parson.
A bed. CANT.
A private dwelling-house. CANT.
A house to lie in. CANT.

To beat; also to wash, or to paint slightly over. I'll give you a good lick o' the chops; I'll give you a good stroke or blow on the face. Jack tumbled into a cow t--d, and nastied his best clothes, for which his father stept up, and licked him neatly.--I'll lick you! the dovetail to which is, If you lick me all over, you won't miss--.
A parasite, or talebearer.

To give one a lift; to assist. A good hand at a dead lift; a good hand upon an emergency. To lift one's hand to one's head; to drink to excess, or to drink drams. To lift or raise one's elbow; the same.
See SHOPLIFTER, &c.
A crutch.
A bed. See LIB.
A soldier of the light infantry company.
Thievish, apt to pilfer.
A man with a red fiery nose.
Lice; the light troops are in full march; the lice are crawling about.
The day. CANT.
Gin. A flash of lightning; a glass of gin.
A phrase used by thieves when the officers or turnkeys are examining their countenance. As the traps are taking our likeness; the officers are attentively observing us.
A chimney-sweeper.
(WHIP SLANG) A white driving hat.
Duke of limbs; a tall awkward fellow.
An inferior or pettyfogging attorney.
A prison, confinement.
A dram of brandy.
To get a man into a line, i.e. to divert his attention by a ridiculous or absurd story. To humbug.
Taylors.

To tip the lion; to squeeze the nose of the party tipped, flat to his face with the thumb. To shew the lions and tombs; to point out the particular curiosities of any place, to act the ciceroni: an allusion to Westminster Abbey, and the Tower, where the tombs and lions are shewn. A lion is also a name given by the gownsmen of Oxford to an inhabitant or visitor. It is a standing joke among the city wits to send boys and country folks, on the first of April, to the Tower-ditch, to see the lions washed.
A familiar appellation used to a little boy.
A young chimney-sweeper.
A small dark cell in Guildhall, London, where disorderly apprentices are confined by the city chamberlain: it is called Little Ease from its being so low that a lad cannot stand upright in it.
A term used by sailors, to signify all landsmen on board their ships.
Lice or fleas.
To be in bad loaf, to be in a disagreeable situation, or in trouble.
A till in a tradesman's shop. To frisk a lob; to rob a till. See FLASH PANNEY.
Going on the lob; going into a shop to get change for gold, and secreting some of the change.

A prison. Dr. Grey, in his notes on Hudibras, explains it to allude to one Doctor Lob, a dissenting preacher, who used to hold forth when conventicles were prohibited, and had made himself a retreat by means of a trap door at the bottom of his pulpit. Once being pursued by the officers of justice, they followed him through divers subterraneous passages, till they got into a dark cell, from whence they could not find their way out, but calling to some of their companions, swore they had got into Lob's Pound.
A house to lie in: also a lodging.
A nick name for the surgeon's servant on board a man of war, sometimes for the surgeon himself: from the water gruel prescribed to the sick, which is called loblolley.
A society which met at Lob Hall, at the King and Queen, Norton Falgate, by order of Lob the great.
A dish much eaten at sea, composed of salt beef, biscuit and onions, well peppered, and stewed together.
A scheme, a mode. I must fight that lock; I must try that scheme.
Character. He stood a queer lock; he bore but an indifferent character. A lock is also a buyer of stolen goods, as well as the receptacle for them.
Thin-faced, or lanthorn-jawed. See LANTHORN JAWED.

A blockhead, or stupid fellow. We three loggerheads be: a sentence frequently written under two heads, and the reader by repeating it makes himself the third. A loggerhead is also a double-headed, or bar shot of iron. To go to loggerheads; to fall to fighting.
To lean with one's elbows on a table.
A lazy, idle drone.
Sick of the lombard fever; i.e. of the idles.
A hare; a term used by poachers.
Great. A long price; a great price.
Throwing, or rather trundling, the dice the whole length of the board.
A long-legged person.
A voracious appetite.
A long-winded parson; one who preached long, tedious sermons. A long-winded paymaster; one who takes long credit.
For the good of the loo; for the benefit of the company or community.
An awkward, ignorant fellow.

entries.word: LOOKING AS IF ONE COULD NOT HELP IT
entries.text: Looking like a simpleton, or as if one could not say boh! to a goose.
A country bumkin, or clown.
Thirteen pence halfpenny.
An opening, or means of escape. To find a loophole in an act of parliament; i.e. a method of evading it,
Uneven, having one side larger or heavier than the other: boys' paper kites are often said to be lop-sided.
To leap, to run away. He loped down the dancers; he ran down stairs.
A gentleman's companion. He will never louse a grey head of his own; he will never live to be old.
A loitering place, or gossiping shop.
A black bag worn to the hair or wig.
The round house, cage, or any other place of confinement.
A stitch fallen in a stocking.
A small toothed comb.
A clumsy stupid fellow.
Stealing oxen or cows.
A footpad.
Money. Cant.
An awkward fellow: a name given by sailors to landsmen.
To tread in a surreverence, to be bewrayed: an allusion to the proverb, Sh-tt-n luck is good luck.
Ludgate prison.
Ears or wattles. See WATTLES.
Wet linen. Cant.
Thieves who steal wet linen. Cant.
Too much.
Live lumber; soldiers or passengers on board a ship are so called by the sailors.
A club or society of citizens of London.
A house appropriated by thieves for the reception of their stolen property.
To beat; also to include a number of articles under one head.
To be transported.
Persons who contract to unload ships; also thieves who lurk about wharfs to pilfer goods from ships, lighters, &c.
Harlequin.
To be left in the lurch; to be abandoned by one's confederates or party, to be left in a scrape.
Those who lose a game of whist, without scoring five, are said to be lurched.
A lurcher of the law; a bum bailiff, or his setter.
Money, watches, rings, or other moveables.
Strong beer.
To drink.
Drunk. The rolling kiddeys hud a spree, and got bloody lushey; the dashing lads went on a party of pleasure, and got very drunk.
Chamber lye; urine.
A swindler, a sharper, a cheat. On the mace; to live by swindling.
Stolen. CANT.
A halfpenny.
A tallow-chandler.
Whimsical, capricious.
A halfpenny. CANT.
A small candle: a term applied to a little slender man.
A military term for one who, under pretence of sickness, evades his duty.
One in a dismal garb.
A horse racer, or jockey.
Robbing Peter to pay Paul, i.e. borrowing of one man to pay another.
A knowing man.
Liquors prepared from materials of English growth.
He has found a mare's nest, and is laughing at the eggs; said of one who laughs without any apparent cause.
An empty bottle: marine officers being held useless by the seamen. SEA WIT.
A spoil sport.
Persons chained or handcuffed together, in order to be conveyed to gaol, or on board the lighters for transportation, are in the cant language said to be married together.
A sham sore above the elbow, to counterfeit a broken arm by a fall from a scaffold.
A gardener.
A baker.
One who pawns his clothes to purchase liquor.
Crying drunk: perhaps from Mary Magdalene, called Maudlin, who is always painted in tears.
Extremely drunk, or soundly beaten.
Scolding.
Asking or begging. CANT:
A hand. Tip us your mawley; shake hands. with me. Fam the mawley; shake hands.
A filthy composition, sufficient to provoke vomiting.
Gin.
May bees don't fly all the year long; an answer to any one who prefaces a proposition with, It may be.
Over-modest or backward in speech.
A fruit, vulgarly called an open a-se; of which it is more truly than delicately said, that it is never ripe till it is as rotten as a t--d, and then it is not worth a f--t.
Almost drunk.
To spend. Will you melt a borde? will you spend a shilling? The cull melted a couple of decusses upon us; the gentleman spent a couple of crowns upon us. CANT.
Hired bail, so called from having straw stuck in their shoes to distinguish them.
MERRYMAN. The jack pudding, jester, or zany of a mountebank, usually dressed in a party-coloured coat.
A knowing man.
One who eats at the same mess, companion or comrade.
Bold, courageous.
Hip, Michael, your head's on fire. See HYP.
A sheep's heart and pluck.
One who is easily tricked out of his property; a term used by gaolers, for prisoners who have money and bleed freely.
To endeavour at impossibilities.
A boxer. How the milling cove served the cull out; how the boxer beat the fellow.
A chisel.

To rob; also to break, beat out, or kill. I'll mill your glaze; I'll beat out your eye. To mill a bleating cheat; to kill a sheep. To mill a ken; to rob a house. To mill doll; to beat hemp in bridewell. CANT.
To force open the doors of houses in order to rob them.
A murderer.
An answer to the offer of any thing inadequate to the purpose for which it is wanted, just as a bandbox would be if used for a seat.
Young chimney sweepers.
Gold. A mint of money; common phrase for a large sum.
A nick name for a cheesemonger: from the small insect of that name found in cheese.
A silversmith.
Bailiffs, or Philistines.
The mob: a sort of opposite to nobility.

A man in the civil line, a townsman, or tradesman: a military term, from the mohair buttons worn by persons of those descriptions, or any others not in the army, the buttons of military men being always of metal: this is generally used as a term of contempt, meaning a bourgeois, tradesman, or mechanic.
Half, but vulgarly used to signify a share or portion: as, He will come in for a small moiety.
M. T. i.e. empty: as, Take away this bottle, it has Moll Thompson's mark upon it.
Saint Monday. See SAINT.

Cheats who drop money, which they pretend to find just before some country lad; and by way of giving him a share of their good luck, entice him into a public house, where they and their confederates cheat or rob him of what money he has about him.
Terms used by printers: monks are sheets where the letters are blotted, or printed too black; friars, those letters where the ink has failed touching the type, which are therefore white or faint.

To suck the monkey; to suck or draw wine, or any other liquor, privately out of a cask, by means of a straw, or small tube. Monkey's allowance; more kicks than halfpence. Who put that monkey on horseback without tying his legs? vulgar wit on a bad horseman.

A link-boy: link-boys are said to curse the moon, because it renders their assistance unnecessary; these gentry frequently, under colour of lighting passengers over kennels, or through dark passages, assist in robbing them. Cant.
A kind of annual fair in the west of England, where farmers usually hire their servants.
To drink up. To empty a glass or pot.
Stupid, melancholy for want of society.
Money.
A brown bill, or kind of halbert, formerly carried by watchmen; corruption of MORE, great or broad, and GLAVE, blade.
The gallows. He napped the king's pardon and escaped the morning drop; he was pardoned, and was not hanged.
Come, morris off; dance off, or get you gone. allusion to morris, i.e. MORISCO, or Moorish dancing.
A cant term for lead, because both are found on the tops of buildings.
Rings, watches, or any toys of value.
To speak like a mouse in a cheese; i.e. faintly or indistinctly.
The parson's mousetrap; the state of matrimony.
A silly fellow. A dupe. To stand mouth; i.e. to be duped.
A drover: from their frequent sleeping on hay mows. CANT.
A cow.
Money; also dung.
A miser.
A fool, or thick-sculled fellow; also, among printers the same as dung among journeymen taylors. See DUNG.
A fellow who goes about by the water side picking up coals, nails, or other articles in the mud. Also a duck.
A napkin.
The sect or disciples of Lodowick Muggleton.
Sick of the mulligrubs with eating chopped hay: low-spirited, having an imaginary sickness.
An ancient game like hazard, played with dice: probably so named from the silence observed in playing at it.
The monument erected on Fish-street Hill, London, in memory of the great fire in 1666.
The mouth.
Originally beggars of the genteel kind, but since used for beggars in general.
An alehouse where beggars are harboured.
To beg.
He looked like God's revenge against murder; he looked angrily.
A person or family suddenly raised to riches and eminence: an allusion to that fungus, which starts up in a night.
Stupid.
A beard.
A violent blow on the mouth. The milling cove tipped the cull a muzzler; the boxer gave the fellow a blow on the mouth.
See MINT.
The constable's assistants, watchmen, &c.
A hat. Penthouse nab; a large hat.

To seize, or catch unawares. To nab the teaze; to be privately whipped. To nab the stoop; to stand in the pillory. To nab the rust; a jockey term for a horse that becomes restive. To nab the snow: to steal linen left out to bleach or dry. CANT.

entries.word: To NAB GIRDER, or NOB GIRDER
entries.text: A bridle.
To have a nack; to be ready at any thing, to have a turn-for it.
Ingenious.
Secured, fixed. He offered me a decus, and I nailed him; he offered me a crown, and I struck or fixed him.
To take any one napping; i.e. to come upon him unexpectedly, to find him asleep: as, He caught him napping, as Morse caught his mare.
The head; also a cheat or thief.
A sheep stealer. CANT.
Strong ale.
A prison or bridewell. The new nask; Clerkenwell bridewell. Tothil-fields nask; the bridewell at Tothil-fields. CANT.
An abbreviation of damnation: a vulgar term used in Kent, Sussex, and the adjacent counties, for very. Nation good; very good. A nation long way; a very long way.
Young thieves or pickpockets. CANT.
The Fleet prison. Commander of the Fleet; the warden of the Fleet prison.
A bye-word, proverb.
The foretop of a wig made in imitation of Christ's head of hair, as represented by the painters and sculptors.
The boy who collects the pots belonging to an alehouse, sent out with beer to private houses.

Formerly the persons claiming the benefit of clergy were obliged to read a verse in a Latin manuscript psalter: this saving them from the gallows, was termed their neck verse: it was the first verse of the fiftyfirst psalm, Miserere mei,&c.
Hemp.
A sharper.
Golden scholars, silver bachelors, and leaden masters.
The scaffold used at Newgate for hanging of criminals; which dropping down, leaves them suspended. By this improvement, the use of that vulgar vehicle, a cart, is entirely left off.
A thief or sharper, frequently caged in Newgate.
A petty fogging and roguish attorney, who attends the gaols to assist villains in evading justice.
The gallows.
Newgate.
Newgate.
To win at dice, to hit the mark just in the nick of time, or at the critical moment.
Old nick; the Devil.
A simpleton.
Toys, baubles, or curiosities. NlCKNACKATORY. A toyshop.
A trifler.
A constable.

A soldier who, as the term is, sings out at the halberts. It is a point of honour in some regiments, among the grenadiers, never to cry out, become nightingales, whilst under the discipline of the cat of nine tails; to avoid which, they chew a bullet.
One whose business it is to empty necessary houses in London, which is always done in the night; the operation is called a wedding. See WEDDING.
A simpleton.
A cheat. Bung nipper; a cutpurse.

A nick name for the purser of a ship: from those gentlemen being supposed sometimes to nip, or diminish, the allowance of the seamen, in that and every other article. It is also applied to stingy persons in general.
A small measure.
The sheers used in clipping money.
i.e. SQUEEZER. A hair-dresser.
Nothing.
A king. A man of rank.
The head.
A peruke-maker.
A dull simple fellow.
He is gone to the land of nod; he is asleep.
The head.
Stealing brass knockers from doors.

A ninny, or fool. John-a-Nokes and Tom-a-Stiles; two honest peaceable gentlemen, repeatedly set together by the ears by lawyers of different denominations: two fictitious names formerly used in law proceedings, but now very seldom, having for several years past been supplanted by two other honest peaceable gentlemen, namely, John Doe and Richard Roe.
Old Noll; Oliver Cromwell.
One that is unequalled: frequently applied ironically.
Melting butter in a wig.
Married, hanged.
A blow: as, I took him a nope on the costard.
Spurs; that place, like Rippon, being famous for making them.
Lord Northumberland's arms; a black eye: so called in the last century.
The pillory, usually made of Norway fir.

As plain as the nose on your face; evidently to be seen. He is led by the nose; he is governed. To follow one's nose; to go strait forward. To put one's nose out of joint; to rival one in the favour of any person. To make a bridge of any one's nose; to pass by him in drinking. To nose a stink; to smell it. He cut off his nose to be revenged of his face; said of one who, to be revenged on his neighbour, has materially injured himself.
A man who informs or turns king's evidence.
To give evidence. To inform. His pall nosed and he was twisted for a crack; his confederate turned king's evidence, and he was hanged for burglary.
To bully.

A bag fastened to the horse's head, in which the soldiers of the cavalry put the oats given to their horses: whence the saying, I see the hose bag in his face; i.e. he has been a private man, or rode private.
A nun.
A medicine prepared by particular persons only, a quack medicine.
He changed his note; he told another sort of a story.
The head.
Hanging. Nubbing cheat: the gallows. Nubbing cove; the hangman. Nubbing ken; the sessions house.
An endearing word: as, My dear nug; my dear love.
To beat: as, He nulled him heartily.
To consult the book of numbers: a term used in the House of Commons, when, instead of answering or confuting a pressing argument, the minister calls for a division, i.e. puts the matter to the vote.
A stupid fellow.
A sham collar, to be worn over a dirty shirt.
To cheat: as, they nursed him out of it. An estate in the hands of trustees, for the payment of bdebts, is said to be at nurse.
It was nuts for them; i.e. it was very agreeable to them.
The pillory: as, The cull peeped through the nutcrackers.
A half pint, a nip of ale: whence the nipperkin, a small vessel.
The Peacock in Gray's Inn Lane, where Burton ale is sold in nyps.

I'll make you sing O be joyful on the other side of your mouth; a threat, implying the party threatened will be made to cry. To sing O be easy; to appear contented when one has cause to complain, and dare not.
A silly fellow.
Simple.

A rich maa, a man of good substance and credit. To sport oak; to shut the outward door of a student's room at college. An oaken towel; an oaken cudgel. To rub a man down with an oaken towel; to beat him.
He has sowed his wild oats; he is staid, or sober, having left off his wild tricks.
To put in one's oar; to intermeddle, or give an opinion unasked: as, To be sure, you must put in your oar!
Vulgar misnomer of OBSTREPEROUS: as, I was going my rounds, and found this here gemman very obstropulous, whereof I comprehended him as an auspicious parson.
I'll do it one of these odd-come-shortly's; I will do it some time or another.
To give the office; to give information, or make signs to the officers to take a thief.
Eyes. Rum ogles; fine eyes.

entries.word: OIL OF BARLEY, or BARLEY BROTH
entries.text: Strong beer.
I will anoint you with the oil of gladness; ironically spoken for, I will beat you.
Ugly. CANT.
Expert, accustomed.
Knowing or expert in any business.
A composition used by vintners to adulterate their wines; also the nick-name for the devil.
See OLD HAT.
GORY. A piece of gold.
The Devil: from NEKEN, the evil spirit of the north.
The Devil. Likewise an expression of quizzical familiarity, as "how d'ye do, OLD ONE?"
The Devil.
One accustomed to business, one who knows mankind.
A brisk old fellow. CANT.
Bridewell.
A chamber pot.
The name of one of the principal rogues of the canting crew. CANT.
The whole together: jocular imitation of law Latin.
A parson: an allusion to his tithes.

A seal. Onion hunters, a class of young thieves who are on the look out for gentlemen who wear their seals suspended on a ribbon, which they cut, and thus secure the seals or other trinkets suspended to the watch.
A medlar. See MEDLAR.
The senior and junior optimes are the second and last classes of Cambridge honors conferred on taking a degree. That of wranglers is the first. The last junior optime is called the Wooden Spoon.
Bone-handled knives. CANT.
Oatstealer.
The vulgar word for a skeleton.
A man standing in the pillory, is, from his elevated situation, said to be made an overseer.

entries.word: OUT AT HEELS, OR OUT AT ELBOWS
entries.text: In declining circumstances.
A man who has lived above his means, or income, is said to have outrun the constable.
A gentleman of three outs. See GENTLEMAN.

To catch the; a trick practised upon ignorant country boobies, who are decoyed into a barn under pretence of catching an owl, where, after divers preliminaries, the joke ends in their having a pail of water poured upon their heads.
Corruption of oyez, proclaimed by the crier of all courts of justice.
A gob of thick phlegm, spit by a consumptive man; in law Latin, UNUM VIRIDUM GOBBUM

To mind one's P's and Q's; to be attentive to the main chance. P.P.C. An inscription on the visiting cards of our modern fine gentleman, signifying that they have called POUR PRENDRE CONGE, i.e. 'to take leave,' This has of late been ridiculed by cards inscribed D.I.O. i.e. 'Damme, I'm off.'
A false report.
The highway, or a robber thereon; also a bed. Footpads; foot robbers. To go out upon the pad; to go out in order to commit a robbery.
Horse stealers.
See To BEAT THE HOOF.
An execution day, Tyburn being in the parish or neighbourhood of Paddington. To dance the Paddington frisk; to be hanged.
I'll cut your painter for you; I'll send you off; the painter being the ropfe that holds the boat fast to the ship. SEA TERM.
Oars. CANT.
A companion. One who generally accompanies another, or who commit robberies together.
The knave of clubs.
Bread.

A servant belonging to the Temple and Gray's Inn, whose office is to announce the dinner. This in the Temple, is done by blowing a horn; and in Gray's Inn proclaiming the word Manger, Manger, Manger, in each of the three courts.
A hart: that animal is, in the Psalms, said to pant after the fresh water-brooks. Also the human heart, which frequently pants in time of danger. CANT.
A butler.
A thin-scull'd foolish fellow.
Milk pottage.
Whites of eggs, bay salt, milk, and pump water, beat together, and poured into a vessel of wine to prevent its fretting.
To put a man's nose into a parenthesis: to pull it, the fingers and thumb answering the hooks or crochets. A wooden parenthesis; the pillory. An iron parenthesis; a prison.
The chippings of money. CANT.
His stockings are of two parishes; i.e. they are not fellows.
A jeering name for a militiaman: from substitutes being frequently hired by the parish from which one of its inhabitants is drawn.
Teeth.
A curate.
A jocular name, or term of reproach, to one who stops the circulation of the glass by preaching over his liquor; as it is said was done by a parson of that name whose cellar was under his pulpit.
Inclining more to one side than the other, crooked, all o' one hugh.
A camp game with three dice: doublets, making up ten or more, to pass or win; any other chances lose.
Apposite, or to the purpose.
The head. Carroty-pated; red-haired.

The fifteenth rank of the canting tribe; strolling priests that marry people under a hedge, without gospel or common prayer book: the couple standing on each side of a dead beast, are bid to live together till death them does part; so shaking hands, the wedding is ended. Also any minister or parson.
The maundering or pert replies of servants; also talk or palaver in order to amuse one intended to be cheated. Pattering of prayers; the confused sound of a number of persons praying together.
The street.
To conceal in the hand. To paum a die: to hide a die in the palm of the hand. He paums; he cheats. Don't pretend to paum that upon me.
A hand or foot; look at his dirty paws. Fore paw; the hand. Hind paw; the foot. To paw; to touch or handle clumsily.

To smear over. To pay the bottom of a ship or boat; to smear it over with pitch: The devil to pay, and no pitch hot or ready. SEA TERM.--Also to beat: as, I will pay you as Paul paid the Ephesians, over the face and eyes, and all your d---d jaws. To pay away; to fight manfully, also to eat voraciously. To pay through the nose: to pay an extravagant price.
To impeach: called also to blow the gab, squeak, or turn stag.
Any kind of lace.

Taking bounties from several regiments and immediately deserting. The cove was fined in the steel for pear making; the fellow was imprisoned in the house of correction for taking bounties from different regiments.
To cry peccavi; to acknowledge one's self in an error, to own a fault: from the Latin PECCAVI, I have sinned.
Victuals. Peck and booze; victuals and drink.
Hungry.
A basket. CANT.
To strip: allusion to the taking off the coat or rind of an orange or apple.
A spying glass; also a looking-glass. Track up the dancers, and pike with the peeper; whip up stairs, and run off with the looking-glass. CANT.
Drowsy.
To look about, to be circumspect.
Inquisitive, suspicious. The cull's peery; that fellow suspects something. There's a peery, tis snitch we are observed, there's nothing to be done.
Gone to Peg Trantum's; dead.
Tumultuously, helter skelter, jumbled together.
A heat, chafe, or passion; as, What a pelt he was in! Pelt is also the skin of several beasts.
The pillory.
Saving in small matters, and extravagant in great.
An equivalent. A good pennyworth; cheap bargain.
A broad brimmed hat.
Warm, passionate.
Water cyder.
A wig.
In a pet; in a passion or miff.

A portmanteau or cloke-bag. Biter of peters; one that makes it a trade to steal boxes and trunks from behind stage coaches or out of waggons. To rob Peter to pay Paul; to borrow of one man to pay another: styled also manoeuvring the apostles.
will kill all the birds that died last summer. A piece of wit commonly thrown out at a person walking through a street or village near London, with a gun in his hand.
The department of stealing portmanteaus, trunks, &c.
Who is Peter Lug? who lets the glass stand at his door, or before him.
Passionate.
Strong malt liquor.
Bailiffs, or officers of justice; also drunkards.
Firemen belonging to an insurance office, which gave a badge charged with a phoenix: these men were called likewise firedrakes.
A. bottle of phosphorus: used by housebreakers to light their lanthorns. Ding the phos; throw away the bottle of phosphorus.
Half a quarter of a sheet. See VESSEL, PHYSOG.
The face. A vulgar abbreviation of physiognomy.
The face. Rum phyz; an odd face or countenance.
A pirate; also a sharper.
Pilfering, petty larceny.
A tale-bearer or mischief maker.
The sheriff's picture frame; the gallows or pillory.
To make water: a childish expression; as, Mammy, I want to piddle. Piddling also means trifling, or doing any thing in a small degree: perhaps from peddling.
A police officer. A China street pig; a Bow-street officer. Floor the pig and bolt; knock down the officer and run away.
Obstinate.
A weak silly fellow easily imposed on. To pigeon; to cheat. To milk the pigeon; to attempt impossibilities, to be put to shifts for want of money. To fly a blue pigeon; to steal lead off a church.
Boys and novices are frequently sent on the first of April to buy pigeons milk.
To run away. Pike off; run away.
A sirreverence, human excrement.

In or to a merry pin; almost drunk: an allusion to a sort of tankard, formerly used in the north, having silver pegs or pins set at equal distances from the top to the bottom: by the rules of good fellowship, every person drinking out of one of these tankards, was to swallow the quantity contained between two pins; if he drank more or less, he was to continue drinking till he ended at a pin: by this means persons unaccustomed to measure their draughts were obliged to drink the whole tankard. Hence when a person was a little elevated with liquor, he was said to have drunk to a merry pin.
At a pinch; on an exigency.

entries.word: To PINCH ON THE PARSON'S SIDE
entries.text: To defraud the parson of his tithe.
A broken winded horse.
A club or brotherhood, A.D. 1743.

He will piss when he can't whistle; he will be hanged. He shall not piss my money against the wall; he shall not have my money to spend in liquor. He who once a good name gets, May piss a bed, and say he sweats.
Discoloured: commonly applied to a discoloured grey wig.
A great drinker, one much given to liquor.
A physician who judges of the diseases of his patients solely by the inspection of their urine.
Flattering him.
A watch fob. He drew a rare thimble from the swell's pit. He took a handsome watch from the gentleman's fob.
A window stopt up on the inside, to save the tax imposed in that gentleman's administration. PARTY WIT
The palpitation of the heart: as, my heart went pit-a-pat. Pintledy-pantledy; the same.
Stuck fast, confounded.
A society held, A. D, 1744, at the sign of the Tower, on Tower Hill: president, Don Pizzaro.
The place in the house of the fence where stolen goods are secreted. Any place where stolen goods are concealed.
To lay, place, or hide. Plant your wids and stow them; be careful what you say, or let slip. Also to bury, as, he was planted by the parson.
Broad-faced.

To play booty; to play with an intention to lose. To play the whole game; to cheat. To play least in sight; to hide, or keep out of the way. To play the devil; to be guilty of some great irregularity or mismanagement.
An hundred thousand pounds.
It is all plummy; i.e. all is right, or as it ought to be.
I am not plump currant; I am out of sorts.
A crutch; also a trader.
Drunk.

To stretch a point; to exceed some usual limit, to take a great stride. Breeches were usually tied up with points, a kind of short laces, formerly given away by the churchwardens at Whitsuntide, under the denomination of tags: by taking a great stride these were stretched.
A blow with the fist: I'll lend you a poke. A poke likewise means a sack: whence, to buy a pig in a poke, i.e. to buy any thing without seeing or properly examining it.
He is like a rope-dancer's polo, lead at both ends; a saying of a stupid sluggish fellow.

To polish the king's iron with one's eyebrows; to be in gaol, and look through the iron grated windows. To polish a bone; to eat a meal. Come and polish a bone with me; come and eat a dinner or supper with me.
The head, jolly nob, napper, or knowledge box; also a wig.
A blow. Lend him a polt in the muns; give him a knock in the face.
Aqua pompaginis; pump water. See AQUA.
Money. Post the poney; lay down the money.

Pistols. Popshop: a pawnbroker's shop. To pop; to pawn: also to shoot. I popped my tatler; I pawned my watch. I popt the cull; I shot the man. His means are two pops and a galloper; that is, he is a highwayman.
Pottage. CANT.
To cry pork; to give intelligence to the undertaker of a funeral; metaphor borrowed from the raven, whose note sounds like the word pork. Ravens are said to smell carrion at a distance.
Keep your breath to cool your porridge; i. e. held your tongue.

A nosegay. I shall see you ride backwards up Holborn-hill, with a book in one hand, and a posey in t'other; i.e. I shall see you go to be hanged. Malefactors who piqued themselves on being properly equipped for that occasion, had always a nosegay to smell to, and a prayer book, although they could not read.
The mob.
The prime minister, who has the patronage of all posts and places.
A house painter, who occasionally paints or anoints posts. Knight of the post; a false evidence, one ready to swear any thing for hire. From post to pillar; backwards and forwards.
A parson who hurries over the service.
The pot calls the kettle black a-se; one rogue exclaims against another.
On the pot; i.e. at stool.
One who hunts more tor the sake of the prey than the sport. Pot valiant; courageous from drink. Potwallopers: persons entitled to vote in certain boroughs by having boiled a pot there.
A scrawl, bad writing.
A person that guts letters; i.e. opens them and secretes the money. The kiddey was topped for the poultry rig; the young fellow was hanged for secreting a letter and taking out the contents.
A prison. See LOB'S POUND. Pounded; imprisoned. Shut up in the parson's pound; married. POWDER
A boy on board a ship of war, whose business is to fetch powder from the magazine.
Cutting bags from behind horses. CANT.
A horse. The swell flashes a rum prad: the e gentleman sports a fine horse.
A horse. Prancer's nab.; a horse's head, used as a seal to a counterfeit pass. At the sign of the prancer's poll, i.e. the nag's head.
A talkative boy.
The tongue.
Buttocks; also a tinder box. CANT.
Tea. See CHATTER BROTH, SCANDAL BROTH, &c.
The pulpit.
This great and laudable society (as they termed themselves) held their grand chapter at the Coal-hole.
Married.
A thief, a cheat: also a conceited coxcomical fellow.
A thief taker.
Thieves in general. Priggers of prancers; horse stealers. Priggers of cacklers: robbers of hen-roosts.
A rival in love.
I had like to be brought into a priminary; i.e. into trouble; from PREMUNIRE.
When the majesty of the people was a favourite terra in the House of Commons, a celebrated wit, seeing chimney sweepers dancing on a May-day, styled them the young princes.
A pert, lively, forward fellow.
Dressing over nicely: prinked up as if he came out of a bandbox, or fit to sit upon a cupboard's head.
All in print, quite neat or exact, set, screwed up. Quite in print; set in a formal manner.

To break Priscian's head; to write or speak false grammar. Priscian was a famous grammarian, who flourished at Constantinople in the year 525; and who was so devoted to his favourite study, that to speak false Latin in his company, was as disagreeable to him as to break his head.
Provision. Rum prog; choice provision. To prog; to be on the hunt for provision: called in the military term to forage.
To make a property of any one; to make him a conveniency, tool, or cat's paw; to use him as one's own.
He from whom any money is taken on the highway: perhaps provider, or provider. CANT.
Mr. Prunella; a parson: parson's gowns being frequently made of prunella.
To examine minutely into a matter or business. A prying fellow; a man of impertinent curiosity, apt to peep and inquire into other men's secrets.
A bankrupt.
The guts: I'll let out your puddings.
A stupid fellow, one whose brains are all in confusion.
A parson.
In good time, or at the beginning of a meal: pudding formerly making the first dish. To give the crows a pudding; to die. You must eat some cold pudding, to settle your love.
One who bids at auctions, not with an intent to buy, but only to raise the price of the lot; for which purpose many are hired by the proprietor of the goods on sale.

Bidding at an auction, as above; also praising any thing above its merits, from interested motives. The art of puffing is at present greatly practised, and essentially necessary in all trades, professions, and callings. To puff and blow; to be out of breath.
An inferior carpenter, one employed only in small jobs.
Watered cyder.
To be pulled; to be arrested by a police officer. To have a pull is to have an advantage; generally where a person has some superiority at a game of chance or skill.
He was christened in pump water; commonly said of a person that has a red face.
Persons at the universities who make it their business to instruct and superintend a number of pupils.
An affected or conceited coxcomb.
Ale in which wormwood has been infused, or ale and bitters drunk warm.
Canary wine; with a dash of tincture of wormwood.
One that is vain of his riches.
Goods taken up at thrice their value, by young spendthrifts, upon trust.
A bassoon: from its likeness to a syphon, called a purser's pump.
A country put; an ignorant awkward clown. To put upon any one; to attempt to impose on him, or to make him the but of the company.
A lawyer who has a confused understanding.
An ignorant blundering parson.
An ungraduated ignorant pretender to skill in physic, a vender of nostrums.
A mountebank: a seller of salves.
A duck.
Abbreviation of quagmire; marshy moorish around.
A calf or sheep.
A glazier: from the small squares in casements, called CARREUX, vulgarly quarrels.
A body. CANT.

Divided into four parts; to be hanged, drawn, and quartered, is the sentence on traitors and rebels. Persons receiving part of the salary of an office from the holder of it, by virtue of an agreement with the donor, are said to be quartered on him. Soldiers billetted on a publican are likewise said to be quartered on him.
To suppress, annul or overthrow; vulgarly pronounced squash: they squashed the indictment.
Base, roguish, bad, naught or worthless. How queerly the cull touts; how roguishly the fellow looks. It also means odd, uncommon. CANT.
Out of order, without knowing one's disease.
To puzzle or confound. I have queered the old full bottom; i.e. I have puzzled the judge. To queer one's ogles among bruisers; to darken one's day lights.
Large buckles.
Rogues relieved from prison, and returned to their old trade.
Coiners. CANT.
The master of a public-house the resort of rogues and sharpers, a cut-throat inn or alehouse keeper.
An empty purse.
Among strolling players, door-keepers who defraud the company, by falsely checking the number of people in the house.
A putter off, or utterer, of bad money.
A maker of bad money.
A rogue. CANT.
A justice of the peace; also a churl.
An ordinary sword, brass or iron hilted.
A prison. CANT.
A bad pair of breeches.
A felt hat, or other bad hat.
A bad, worn-out, foundered horse; also a cowardly or faint-hearted horse-stealer.
An informer that pretends to be sleeping, and thereby overhears the conversation of thieves in night cellars.
Wrong. Improper. Contrary to one's wish. It is queer street, a cant phrase, to signify that it is wrong or different to our wish.
A quitam horse; one that will both carry and draw. LAW WIT.
To make subtle distinctions; also to play upon words.
More like a bear than a squirrel. Jeeringly said to any one moving sluggishly on a business or errand that requires dispatch.
Cash, money. Can you tip me any quids? can you lend me some money?
A politician: from a character of that name in the farce of the Upholsterer.
A clerk, scribe, or hackney writer.
Choked by a hempen quinsey; hanged.
Girds, taunts, jests.
A complete rogue, one that has sung in different choirs or cages, i.e. gaols. CANT.
Tricks and devices. Quirks in law; subtle distinctions and evasions.
A strange-looking fellow, an odd dog. OXFORD.
Newgate, or any other prison. The dab's in quod; the poor rogue is in prison.
Snack, share, part, proportion, or dividend. Tip me my quota; give me part of the winnings, booty, or plunder. CANT.
A midwife.
Young spendthrifts taking up goods on trust at great prices.
Rent strained to the utmost value. To lie at rack and manger; to be in great disorder.
A gormagon. See GORMAGON.
An appellation given by the gownsmen of the university of Oxford to the inhabitants of that place.
Bank notes. Money in general. The cove has no rag; the fellow has no money.
A farthing.
An ensign.
An inspection of the linen and necessaries of a company of soldiers, commonly made by their officers on Mondays or Saturdays.
Gin, or any other common dram: these liquors seldom failing to reduce those that drink them to rags.
A ragged fellow, one all in tatters, a tatterdemallion.
