Knight of the rainbow; a footman: from being commonly clothed in garments of different colours. A meeting of gentlemen, styled of the most ancient order of the rainbow, was advertised to be held at the Foppington's Head, Moorfields.
To lay up something for a rainy day; to provide against a time of necessity or distress.
A fool.
A he cat.
The arm. The busnapper's kenchin seized my rammer; i.e. the watchman laid hold of my arm. CANT.
To snatch, or tear any thing forcibly from the person.
Out of repair. A ramshackled house; perhaps a corruption of RANSACKED, i.e. plundered.
Stinking, rammish, ill-flavoured; also strong, great. A rank knave; a rank coward: perhaps the latter may allude to an ill savour caused by fear.
A highwayman.
A swinging great lie.
Of these there are the following kinds: a black rat and a grey rat, a py-rat and a cu-rat.
A contemptuous name for any curious portable piece of machinery, or philosophical apparatus.
A coach. Rattle and prad; a coach and horses.
A coachman. CANT.
Beggars who ply coaches. CANT.
A bull beggar, or scarechild, with which foolish nurses terrify crying brats.
The ready rhino; money. CANT.
A riddle or pun on a man's name, expressed in sculpture or painting, thus: a bolt or arrow, and a tun, for Bolton; death's head, and a ton, for Morton.
To reckon with one's host; to make an erroneous judgment in one's own favour. To cast-up one's reckoning or accounts; to vomit.
To get a fresh supply of money.
Robbing on the highway.
Port wine.
The throat. Gone down the red lane; swallowed.
Brandy.
A public house.
The tongue. Shut your potatoe trap, and give your red rag a holiday; i.e. shut your mouth, and let your tongue rest. Too much of the red rag (too much tongue).

Share of the booty. The coves cracked the swell's crib, fenced the swag, and each cracksman napped his regular; some fellows broke open a gentleman's house, and after selling the property which they had stolen, they divided the money between them.
One much given to prayer, or apt to be down upon his knees.
One who does not break the commandment which prohibits the making of the likeness of any thing in heaven or earth, or in the waters under the earth.
The sign of the Cheshire cheese.

A place of meeting. The rendezvous of the beggars were, about the year 1638, according to the Bellman, St. Quinton's, the Three Crowns in the Vintry, St. Tybs, and at Knapsbury: there were four barns within a mile of London. In Middlesex were four other harbours, called Draw the Pudding out of the Fire, the Cross Keys in Craneford parish, St. Julian's in Isleworth parish, and the house of Pettie in Northall parish. In Kent, the King's Barn near Dartford, and Ketbrooke near Blackheath.
A lock-up or spunging-house, a gaol. Also livery stables where horses and carriages are sold by auction.

An ancient custom, which obliges any person easing himself near the highway or foot-path, on the word REVERENCE being given him by a passenger, to take off his hat with his teeth, and without moving from his station to throw it over his head, by which it frequently falls into the excrement; this was considered as a punishment for the breach of delicacy, A person refusing to obey this law, might be pushed backwards. Hence, perhaps, the term, SIR-REVERENCE.
A man set by bullies on his head, that his money may fall out of his breeches, which they afterwards by accident pick up. See HOISTING.
A visitation of the clergy. See CROW FAIR.
Money. CANT.
Vulgar abusive language, such as was spoken by ribalds. Ribalds were originally mercenary soldiers who travelled about, serving any master far pay, but afterwards degenerated into a mere banditti.
Money. The ribbin runs thick; i.e. there is plenty of money. CANT. Blue ribbin. Gin. The cull lushes the blue ribbin; the silly fellow drinks common gin.
To beat: I'll ribroast him to his heart's content.

A dictionary. A country lad, having been reproved for calling persons by their christian names, being sent by his master to borrow a dictionary, thought to shew his breeding by asking for a Richard Snary.

A person who receives part of the salary of a place or appointment from the ostensible occupier, by virtue of an agreement with the donor, or great man appointing. The rider is said to be quartered upon the possessor, who often has one or more persons thus riding behind him. See QUARTERED.
Fun, game, diversion, or trick. To run one's rig upon any particular person; to make him a butt. I am up to your rig; I am a match for your tricks.
All right! A favourite expression among thieves, to signify that all is as they wish, or proper for their purpose. All right, hand down the jemmy; every thing is in proper order, give me the crow.
Roundabout, nonsensical. He told a long rigmarole story.
When a person receives silver in change to shift some good shillings and put bad ones in their place. The person who gave the change is then requested to give good shillings for these bad ones.
A miserable rip; a poor, lean, worn-out horse. A shabby mean fellow.
Oratorios and operas.
A noisy, riotous fellow.
A broken-winded horse.
A quick trade.

To arrest. I'll roast the dab; I'll arrest the rascal.--Also to jeer, ridicule, or banter. He stood the roast; he was the butt.--Roast meat clothes; Sunday or holiday-clothes. To cry roast meat; to boast of one's situation. To rule the roast; to be master or paramount.
A nick name for the Life Guards, who are mostly substantial house-keepers; and eat daily of roast and boiled.
The third old rank of the canting crew, mighty thieves, like Robin Hood.
with one eye and a stinking breath. The breech.
He was rocked in a stone kitchen; a saying meant to convey the idea that the person spoken of is a fool, his brains having been disordered by the jumbling of his cradle.

entries.word: ROGER, or TIB OF THE BUTTERY
entries.text: A goose. Cant. Jolly Roger; a flag hoisted by pirates.
The fourth order of canters. A rogue in grain; a great rogue, also a corn chandler. A rogue in spirit; a distiller or brandy merchant.
Watch and ward. Romboyled; sought after with a warrant.
London. Cant.
A cheat: probably from the thievish disposition of the birds of that name. Also the cant name for a crow used in house-breaking. To rook; to cheat, particularly at play.
Stealing poultry.

Under the rose: privately or secretly. The rose was, it is said, sacred to Harpocrates, the God of silence, and therefore frequently placed in the ceilings of rooms destined for the receiving of guests; implying, that whatever was transacted there, should not be made public.
One with a sanguine or fresh-coloured countenance.
A coach, cart, or other wheeled carriage.
Small beer; called beer-a-bumble--will burst one's guts before it will make one tumble.
Pirates, vagabonds.
To lie rough; to lie all night in one's clothes: called also roughing it. Likewise to sleep on the bare deck of a ship, when the person is commonly advised to chuse the softest plank.
Saucepans, frying-paps, poker and tongs, marrow-bones and cleavers, bulls horns, &c. beaten upon and sounded in ludicrous processions.

A number of guineas, from twenty to fifty or more, wrapped up in paper, for the more ready circulation at gaming-tables: sometimes they are inclosed in ivory boxes, made to hold exactly 20, 50, or 100 guineas.
Plain, honest dealing.

A mode of signing remonstrances practised by sailors on board the king's ships, wherein their names are written in a circle, so that it cannot be discovered who first signed it, or was, in other words, the ringleader.
A considerable sum.
An instrument used in housebreaking. This instrument has not been long in use. It will cut a round piece about five inches in diameter out of a shutter or door.
The fundament. Brother round mouth, speaks; he has let a fart.
A modern card meeting at a private house; also an order from the Secretary at War, directing the march and quartering of soldiers.
A disturbance; a term used by the students at Cambridge.
To row in the same boat; to be embarked in the same scheme.
To give a Rowland for an Oliver; to give an equivalent. Rowland and Oliver were two knights famous in romance: the wonderful achievements of the one could only be equalled by those of the other.
Highwaymen who never rob any but rich persons, and that without ill treating them. See SCAMP.
Was held every Monday evening, at seven o'clock, at the Three tuns, near the Hospital Gate, Newgate-street.
A rude boisterous fellow; also a hound that opens on a false scent.

To run away. Don't rub us to the whit; don't send us to Newgate. CANT.--To rub up; to refresh: to rub up one's memory. A rub: an impediment. A rubber; the best two out of three. To win a rubber: to win two games out of three.
Red-faced.
Handcuffs. CANT.
The first rank of canters; also notorious rogues pretending to be maimed soldiers or sailors.
The woods, hedges, or bushes. CANT.
It is all rug; it is all right and safe, the game is secure. CANT.
Asleep. The whole gill is safe at rug; the people of the house are fast asleep.
Fine, good, valuable.
A justice of the peace. CANT.
A clever cheat, a clean trick.
A fat wether sheep. CANT.
A jolly host. CANT.
A young apprentice; also a sharp trick.
Wine, or any other good liquor. Rum boozing welts; bunches of grapes. CANT.
A dexterous fellow at stealing silver tankards from inns and taverns.
A valuable dog. CANT.
A full purse. CANT.
Among butchers, a customer easily imposed on, as to the quality and price of meat. CANT.
A song.
A fine silk, cambric, or holland handkerchief. CANT.
A good purse of gold. CANT.
New money, or medals.
A dexterous or clever rogue.
A handsome sword. CANT.
A dextrous pickpocket. CANT.
Silk, or other fine stockings. CANT.
A vintner. CANT.
An expert picklock.

A jolly handsome fellow; also an odd eccentric fellow; likewise the boldest and stoutest fellows lately among the Alsatians, Minters, Savoyards, and other inhabitants of privileged districts, sent to remove and guard the goods of such bankrupts as intended to take sanctuary in those places. CANT.
See RUM DIVER.
A sharp trick. CANT.
Cheats who tell wonderful stories of their sufferings at sea, or when taken by the Algerines, CANT.
See RUM COLE. CANT.
King or chief of the link-boys. CANT.
Breeches of gold or silver brocade, or richly laced with gold or silver. CANT.
One that counterfeits a fool. CANT
A good hat.
A very rich silly fellow. CANT.
The highway. CANT.
Highwaymen well mounted and armed. CANT.
Fine looking-glasses. CANT.
A fine horse. CANT.
A great booty. CANT.
Westphalia ham. CANT.
A smart fillip on the nose.
Much wine, or good liquor, given among fiddlers. CANT.
See RUM DEGEN.
See RUM DEGEN.
See ROMEVILLE.
See RUM CLOUT.
Rum, water, and sugar; also a prison.
A ward or watch.
Obstreperous.
A riot, quarrel, or confusion.
Snatching goods off a counter, and throwing them to an accomplice, who brushes off with them.
Hawker of newspapers, trials, and dying speeches.
The Brown Bear in Bow-street, Covent Garden, a house of call for thief-takers and runners of the Bow street justices.
Out of use, To nab the rust; to be refractory; properly applied to a restive horse, and figuratively to the human species. To ride rusty; to be sullen; called also to ride grub.
A blunt surly fellow: a jocular misnomer of RESTICUS.
The iron door, or blower, to the mouth of a stove: from a divine of that name, who made himself famous for blowing the coals of dissension in the latter end of the reign of queen Ann.

To saddle the spit; to give a dinner or supper. To saddle one's nose; to wear spectacles. To saddle a place or pension; to oblige the holder to pay a certain portion of his income to some one nominated by the donor. Saddle sick: galled with riding, having lost leather.
A piece of spoilt timber in a coach-maker's shop, like a saint, devoted to the flames.
Never, there being no saint of that name: tomorrow-come-never, when two Sundays come together.
An ox; that Evangelist being always represented with an ox.
A barker. Vide BARKER.
The beggars'sacrament or oath.
Foolish. Silly.
Ham, dried tongue, or some other salted meat, cut thin and put between two slices of bread and butter: said to be a favourite morsel with the Earl of Sandwich.
SANKY, or CENTIPEE'S. A taylor employed by clothiers in making soldier's clothing.
A simple fellow. Sappy; foolish.
A term of familiar raillery, signifying a bold or forward person.

An idle, lounging fellow; by some derived from SANS TERRE; applied to persons, who, having no lands or home, lingered and loitered about. Some derive it from persons devoted to the Holy Land, SAINT TERRE, who loitered about, as waiting for company.
An old saw; an ancient proverbial saying.
A set of mock masons, who, A.D. 1744, made a ludicrous procession in ridicule of the Free Masons.
Mean. Sordid. How scaly the cove is; how mean the fellow is.
An honest, rough, blunt sailor.
A highwayman. Royal scamp: a highwayman who robs civilly. Royal foot scamp; a footpad who behaves in like manner.
To run away hastily.
Tea.
One who has eaten shame and drank after it, or would blush at being ashamed.
One who deserves and has narrowly escaped the gallows, a slip-gibbet, one for whom the gallows is said to groan.
A wild dissolute fellow.
To make one's self scarce; to steal away.
A high red, hired or hack horse: a pun on the word HIRED.
A party of pleasure.
A man void of every principle of honour.

To scour or score off; to run away: perhaps from SCORE; i.e. full speed, or as fast as legs would carry one. Also to wear: chiefly applied to irons, fetters, or handcuffs, because wearing scours them. He will scour the darbies; he will be in fetters. To scour the cramp ring; to wear bolts or fetters, from which, as well as from coffin hinges, rings supposed to prevent the cramp are made.
Riotous bucks, who amuse themselves with breaking windows, beating the watch, and assaulting every person they meet: called scouring the streets.
A college errand-boy at Oxford, called a gyp at Cambridge. Also a watchman or a watch. CANT.
Hanged.
Lean, bony.
A public execution.
A villainous scheme or plan. He whiddles the whole scrap; he discovers the whole plan or scheme.
To get into a scrape; to be involved in a disagreeable business.
A fiddler; also one who scrapes plates for mezzotinto prints.

A mode of expressing dislike to a person, or sermon, practised at Oxford by the students, in scraping their feet against the ground during the preachment; frequently done to testify their disapprobation of a proctor who has been, as they think, too rigorous.
Old Scratch; the Devil: probably from the long and sharp claws with which he is frequently delineated.
Bread sopt in the oil and vinegar in which cucumbers have been sliced.
A bank note. Queer screens; forged bank notes. The cove was twisted for smashing queer screens; the fellow was hanged for uttering forged bank notes.
A skeleton key used by housebreakers to open a lock. To stand on the screw signifies that a door is not bolted, but merely locked.

A scrap or slip of paper. The cully freely blotted the scrip, and tipt me forty hogs; the man freely signed the bond, and gave me forty shillings.--Scrip is also a Change Alley phrase for the last loan or subscription. What does scrip go at for the next rescounters? what does scrip sell for delivered at the next day of settling?
To be tipt the scroby; to be whipt before the justices.
A farthing. CANT.
A low mean fellow, employed in all sorts of dirty work.
The itch.
A head of a house, or master of a college, at the universities.
A boat rowed by one man with a light kind of oar, called a scull; also a one-horse chaise or buggy.
A peruke-maker.
A sailor.
A shark.
One ready to give bond and judgment for goods or money.
Poor, pennyless, stiver-cramped, exhausted.
The eyes. See DAYLIGHTS.
Found guilty. Convicted. Ordered to be punished or transported. To serve a cull out; to beat a man soundly.
To drive or break in. Hand down the Jemmy and send it in; apply the crow to the door, and drive it in.
A dead set: a concerted scheme to defraud a person by gaming.
A bailiff's follower, who, like a setting dog follows and points the game for his master. Also sometimes an exciseman.
To knock down or stun any one. We settled the cull by a stroke on his nob; we stunned the fellow by a blow on the head.
An ill-dressed shabby fellow; also a mean-spirited person.
To shake one's elbow; to game with dice. To shake a cloth in the wind; to be hanged in chains.
A simple fellow.
A WHIP hat, so called from the want of depth in the crown. LILLY SHALLOW, a WHITE Whip hat.
To walk awkwardly. Shamble-legged: one that walks wide, and shuffles about his feet.
Legs, or gams.
To shew one's shapes; to be stript, or made peel, at the whipping-post.
A hat: corruption of CHAPEAU. CANT.
A sharper: perhaps from his preying upon any one he can lay hold of. Also a custom-house officer, or tide-waiter. Sharks; the first order of pickpockets. BOW-STREET TERM, A.D. 1785.

Subtle, acute, quick-witted; also a sharper or cheat, in opposition to a flat, dupe, or gull. Sharp's the word and quick's the motion with him; said of any one very attentive to his own interest, and apt to take all advantages. Sharp set; hungry.
A cheat, one that lives by his wits. Sharpers tools; a fool and false dice.
A cunning shaver; a subtle fellow, one who trims close, an acute cheat. A young shaver; a boy. SEA TERM.
The clippings of money.
Bashful. A sheepish fellow; a bashful or shamefaced fellow. To cast a sheep's eye at any thing; to look wishfully at it.
A drummer.
On the shelf, i.e. pawned.
The hangman.
An execution. To dance at the sheriff's ball, and loll out one's tongue at the company; to be hanged, or go to rest in a horse's night-cap, i.e. a halter.
Handcuffs.
A prison.
The gallows.
To evade or disappoint: to sherk one's duty.
To run away: sherry off.
Shuffling. Tricking. Shifting cove; i.e. a person who lives by tricking.
A term used by sailors, to signify soldiers, passengers, or any landsmen on board.
Irresolute. To stand shilly-shally; to hesitate, or stand in doubt.
A dance. SEA PHRASE.
It shines like a shitten barn door.
Proper, as it ought to be. SEA PHRASE,
Vomiting. Hark ye, friend, have you got a padlock on your a-se, that you sh-te through your teeth? Vulgar address to one vomiting.
A parson who attends a funeral is said to be shod all round, when he receives a hat-band, gloves, and scarf: many shoeings being only partial.
New, or strait shoes. I was in the shoemaker's stocks; i.e. had on a new pair of shoes that were too small for me.
To go skulking about.
To vomit from excess of liquor; called also catting.
A prison. Shopped; confined, imprisoned.
One that steals whilst pretending to purchase goods in a shop.
A dram.
A dinner given after a funeral, to those who have carried the corpse.
A partner to a file. See FILE.
A taylor.
To make use of false pretences, or unfair shifts. A shuffling fellow; a slippery shifting fellow.
Sixpence.
Crooked.
FIVE SHILLINGS. The crown. TEN SHILLINGS. The two crowns. FIFTEEN SHILLINGS. The three crowns.
To silence a man; to knock him down, or stun him. Silence in the court, the cat is pissing; a gird upon any one requiring silence unnecessarily.
Thieves who snatch hoods or bonnets from persons walking in the streets.
Replete with lice. The cove's kickseys are silver laced: the fellow's breeches are covered with lice.
A foolish fellow.
To smile: to simper like a firmity kettle.
Abbreviation of simple Tony or Anthony, a foolish fellow.

Physical herbs; also follies. He must go to Battersea, to be cut for the simples--Battersea is a place famous for its garden grounds, some of which were formerly appropriated to the growing of simples for apothecaries, who at a certain season used to go down to select their stock for the ensuing year, at which time the gardeners were said to cut their simples; whence it became a popular joke to advise young people to go to Battersea, at that time, to have their simples cut, or to be cut for the simples.
To call out; the coves sing out beef; they call out stop thief.
To be humbled, confounded, or abashed, to have little or nothing to say for one's-self.
A very foolish fellow; also a particular kind of nails.
A corkscrew, made by a famous cutler of that name, who lived in a place called Hell, in Dublin; his screws are remarkable for their excellent temper.
The old title for a country parson: as Sir John of Wrotham, mentioned by Shakespeare.
Strong beer.
The sur, or upper loin.
Human excrement, a t--d.
One who, from a desire of being the head of the company, pays the reckoning, or, as the term is, stands squire. See SQUIRE.
One who stays late in company, is said to have his sitting breeches on, or that he will sit longer than a hen.
An attorney, whose fee on several occasions is fixed at that sum.
Left at sixes and sevens: i.e. in confusion; commonly said of a room where the furniture, &c. is scattered about; or of a business left unsettled.
Half a pint. Size of bread and cheese; a certain quantity. Sizings: Cambridge term for the college allowance from the buttery, called at Oxford battles.

(CAMBRIDGE) To sup at one's own expence. If a MAN asks you to SUP, he treats you; if to SIZE, you pay for what you eat--liquors ONLY being provided by the inviter. SIZAR (Cambridge). Formerly students who came to the University for purposes of study and emolument. But at present they are just as gay and dissipated as their fellow collegians. About fifty years ago they were on a footing with the servitors at Oxford, but by the exertions of the present Bishop of Llandaff, who was himself a sizar, they were absolved from all marks of inferiority or of degradation. The chief difference at present between them and the pensioners, consists in the less amount of their college fees. The saving thus made induces many extravagant fellows to become sizars, that they may have more money to lavish on their dogs, pieces, &c.
A cup, or beggar's wooden dish.
Crooked, inclining to one side.
In a bad skin; out of temper, in an ill humour. Thin-skinned: touchy, peevish.
A purse. Frisk the skin of the stephen; empty the money out of the purse. Queer skin; an empty purse.
To skink, is to wait on the company, ring the bell, stir the fire, and snuff the candles; the duty of the youngest officer in the military mess. See BOOTS.
A tanner.
A footman.
To wheedle. CANT.
A joke. A satirical hint.
See SCRIP.

A soldier who by feigned sickness, or other pretences, evades his duty; a sailor who keeps below in time of danger; in the civil line, one who keeps out of the way, when any work is to be done. To skulk; to hide one's self, to avoid labour or duty.
Gin.

Cheats who pretend they were farmers in the isle of Sky, or some other remote place, and were ruined by a flood, hurricane, or some such public calamity: or else called sky farmers from their farms being IN NUBIBUS, 'in the clouds.'
The garret, or upper story.
A parson or lawyer's band.
A trick; also a game at whist lost without scoring one. To slam to a door; to shut it with violence.
A fetter. Double slanged; double ironed. Now double slanged into the cells for a crop he is knocked down; he is double ironed in the condemned cells, and ordered to be hanged.
Cant language.

A petty cook's shop, where there is no credit given, but what is had must be paid DOWN WITH THE READY SLAP-BANG, i.e. immediately. This is a common appellation for a night cellar frequented by thieves, and sometimes for a stage coach or caravan.
Immediately, instantly, suddenly.
Half a crown. CANT.
A sheet. CANT.
The gaol at Kingston in Jamaica: Slater is the deputy Provost-marshal.
A partner in a trade, or shop, who lends his name and money, for which he receives a share of the profit, without doing any part of the business.
Much worn: the cloth of your coat must be extremely sleepy, for it has not had a nap this long time.
A fool's errand, in search of what it is impossible to find.
See SCAPEGALLOWS.
One on whom there can be no dependance, a shuffling fellow.
Tea, water-gruel, or any innocent beverage taken medicinally.
Misnaming and misapplying any hard word; from the character of Mrs. Slipslop, in Fielding's Joseph Andrews.
Wearing apparel and bedding used by seamen.
A dealer in those articles, who keeps a slop shop.
A stooping gait, a negligent slovenly fellow. To slouch; to hang down one's head. A slouched hat: a hat whose brims are let down.
A dirty nasty fellow.
A piece of lead of any shape, to be fired from a blunderbuss. To fire a slug; to drink a dram.
A drone, one that cannot rise in the morning.
Take a hearty drink.
To slur, is a method of cheating at dice: also to cast a reflection on any one's character, to scandalize.
Greasy dish-water, or the skimmings of a pot where fat meat has been boiled.
A foul feeder, one that eats much greasy food.
A cunning fellow, under the mask of simplicity.
Killed in battle.
Level with the surface, every thing cut away.
A coachman.
Breeches: a gird at the affected delicacy of the present age; a suit being called coat, waistcoat, and articles, or small clothes.
Spruce, fine: as smart as a carrot new scraped.
Money allowed to soldiers or sailors for the loss of a limb, or other hurt received in the service.
A person who lives by passing base coin. The cove was fined in the steel for smashing; the fellow was ordered to be imprisoned in the house of correction for uttering base coin.
Leg of mutton and smash: a leg of mutton and mashed turnips. SEA TERM.
To break; also to kick down stairs. CANT. To smash. To pass counterfeit money.
A plasterer.
A nose. Smellers: a cat's whiskers.
An orchard, or garden; also a nosegay. CANT.
Half guineas. CANT.
A finical spruce fellow. To smirk; to smile, or look pleasantly.
An arm. To smite one's tutor; to get money from him. ACADEMIC TERM.
To observe, to suspect.
A tobacconist.
Curious, suspicious, inquisitive.
Dried leaves of the ash tree, used by the smugglers for adulterating the black or bohea teas.
A nick name for a blacksmith; also neat and spruce.

Persons who pretend to be smugglers of lace and valuable articles; these men borrow money of publicans by depositing these goods in their hands; they shortly decamp, and the publican discovers too late that he has been duped; and on opening the pretended treasure, he finds trifling articles of no value.
To snatch, or seize suddenly.
A copper. A grate. Old iron. The cove was lagged for a smut: the fellow was transported for stealing a copper.
A share. To go snacks; to be partners.
To rifle or plunder; also to kill.
A highwayman. Snaffler of prances; a horse stealer.
To steal. To snaffle any ones poll; to steal his wig.
A Christmas gambol: raisins and almonds being put into a bowl of brandy, and the candles extinguished, the spirit is set on fire, and the company scramble for the raisins.
To break shop windows or show glasses.
Pistols.
Taken, caught.

A pilferer. Morning sneak; one who pilfers early in the morning, before it is light. Evening sneak; an evening pilferer. Upright sneak: one who steals pewter pots from the alehouse boys employed to collect them. To go upon the sneak; to steal into houses whose doors are carelessly left open. CANT.
A small bowl.
One that robs alone.
A mean-spirited fellow, a sneaking cur.
Jeering, flickering, laughing in scorn.
A glandered horse.
To laugh privately, or in one's sleeve.
To eye, or look at any thing attentively: the cull snilches. CANT.
A taylor.
To turn snitch, or snitcher; to turn informer.
To wipe, or slap. Snite his snitch; wipe his nose, i.e. give him a good knock.
To cry, to throw the snot or snivel about. Snivelling; crying. A snivelling fellow; one that whines or complains.
To speak through the nose, to snuffle.
A nick name for a shoemaker.
Linen hung out to dry or bleach. Spice the snow; to steal the linen.
A hogshead. CANT.
To check, or rebuke.
A parson.
A thief who hides himself under a bed, in Order to rob the house.
To take snuff; to be offended.
To speak through the nose.
A cold in the head, attended with a running at the nose.
All's snug; all's quiet.
To drink. An old soaker; a drunkard, one that moistens his clay to make it stick together.
A large one.
A pretended soldier, begging with a counterfeit wound, which he pretends to have received at some famous siege or battle.
A piece of tallow candle.
A red herring.
A parish clerk.
A miserable performer on any instrument, who always plays alone, because no one will stay in the room to hear him.
A lawyer.
He changed his song; he altered his account or evidence. It was bought for an old song, i.e. very cheap. His morning and his evening song do not agree; he tells a different story.
A bribe. A sop for Cerberus; a bribe for a porter, turnkey, or gaoler.
(Cambridge) An undergraduate in his second year.
A yellowish red. Sorrel pate; one having red hair.
Tobacco.
The body. He made a hole in his soul case; he wounded him.
A parson.
A herd of swine.
A sucking pig.
A seven shilling piece.
Money; also blows with the open hand.
Large.
A spruce, trim, or smart fellow. A man that is always thirsty, is said to have a spark in his throat.
Fine, gay.
To rob. I spoke with the cull on the cherry-coloured prancer; I robbed the man on the black horse. CANT.
Any thing stolen. He has made a good speak; he has stolen something considerable.
A coloured hankerchief. CANT.
To rob. Spice the swell; rob the gentleman.
A privy. Stink-hole bay or dilberry creek. The fundament.
To confound, silence, or dumbfound.
A small reward or gift.
Thrown from a horse, or overturned in a carriage; pray, coachee, don't spill us.
To kidnap, or inveigle away.
A sword.
A violent, pettish, or passionate person.
Married: an allusion to joining two ropes ends by splicing. SEA TERM.
The sign of the spread eagle, which being represented with two heads on one neck, gives it somewhat the appearance of being split.
A lawyer.
A grocer.
The nick-name for a smith.

To exhibit: as, Jack Jehu sported a new gig yesterday: I shall sport a new suit next week. To sport or flash one's ivory; to shew one's teeth. To sport timber; to keep one's outside door shut; this term is used in the inns of court to signify denying one's self. N.B. The word SPORT was in great vogue ann. 1783 and 1784.

A thirsty fellow, a great drinker. To spunge; to eat and drink at another's cost. Spunging-house: a bailiff's lock-up-house, or repository, to which persons arrested are taken, till they find bail, or have spent all their money: a house where every species of fraud and extortion is practised under the protection of the law.
Rotten touchwood, or a kind of fungus prepared for tinder; figuratively, spirit, courage.
The right hand.
To rehearse theatrically.
A meeting of apprentices and mechanics to rehearse different characters in plays: thus forming recruits for the strolling companies.
Theatrical declamation.
Pawned.
Butter.
A soldier tied to the halberts in order to be whipped; his attitude bearing some likeness to that figure, as painted on signs.
A frolic. Fun. A drinking bout. A party of pleasure.
Honest, not roguish. A square cove, i.e. a man who does not steal, or get his living by dishonest means.
An old man: square toed shoes were anciently worn in common, and long retained by old men.
A narrow escape, a chance: he had a squeak for his life. To squeak; to confess, peach, or turn stag. They squeak beef upon us; they cry out thieves after us. CANT.
A good-natured foolish fellow, ready to become security for another, under hand and seal.
A small satirical or political temporary jeu d'esprit, which, like the firework of that denomination, sparkles, bounces, stinks, and vanishes.
A weak profligate spendthrift, the squire of the company; one who pays the whole reckoning, or treats the company, called standing squire.
Foolish.
See HUNTING.
To turn stag; to impeach one's confederates: from a herd of deer, who are said to turn their horns against any of their number who is hunted.
To find, discover, or observe.

Making or ordaining. Stalling to the rogue; an ancient ceremony of instituting a candidate into the society of rogues, somewhat similar to the creation of a herald at arms. It is thus described by Harman: the upright man taking a gage of bowse, i.e. a pot of strong drink, pours it on the head of the rogue to be admitted; saying,--I, A.B. do stall thee B.C. to the rogue; and from henceforth it shall be lawful for thee to cant for thy living in all places.
A broker's shop, or that of a receiver of stolen goods.
To cant. CANT.
A particular manner of throwing the dice out of the box, by striking it with violence against the table.
Legs.
Shoes.
He was run to a stand-still; i.e. till he could no longer move.
To break and rob a jeweller's show glass. CANT.
Stiff, prim, formal, affected.
An ox cheek.
Newgate: he is gone to the start, or the old start. CANT.
One who leaves a jolly company, a milksop; he is no starter, he will sit longer than a hen.
Breaking shop-windows, and stealing some article thereout.
To stop. To finish. To end. The cove tipped the prosecutor fifty quid to stash the business; he gave the prosecutor fifty guineas to stop the prosecution.
A taylor; from that article, and its coadjutor buckram, which make no small figure in the bills of those knights of the needle.
A pipe. A swell steamer; a long pipe, such as is used by gentlemen to smoke.
The house of correction.
A needle. A steel bar flinger; a taylor, stay-maker, or any other person using a needle.
Money. Stephen's at home; i.e. has money.
A decoction of raisins of the sun and lemons in conduit water, sweetened with sugar, and bottled up.
Household furniture.
Pops or pistols. Stow your sticks; hide your pistols. CANT. See POPS.
A pair of gloves.
Proud, stately.
Strong beer, or other liquor.
A parting cup or glass, drank on horseback by the person taking leave.
Strong ale.
A good stock; i.e. of impudence. Stock and block; the whole: he has lost stock and block.
Stockings.
The stomach worm gnaws; I am hungry.
Newgate, or any other prison.
Ditto.

entries.word: STOOP-NAPPERS, or OVERSEERS OF THE NEW PAVEMENT
entries.text: Persons set in the pillory. CANT.
The pillory. The cull was served for macing and napp'd the stoop; he was convicted of swindling, and put in the pillory.
A great blow. Tip him a stoter in the haltering place; give him a blow under the left ear.
A vessel to hold liquor: a vessel containing a size or half a pint, is so called at Cambridge.
Stow you; be silent, or hold your peace. Stow your whidds and plant'em, for the cove of the ken can cant'em; you have said enough, the man of the house understands you.
Precise, over nice, puritanical.
See STAMMEL.
A poulterer.
To work. The kiddy would not strap, so he went on the scamp: the lad would not work, and therefore robbed on the highway.
Hanging. He'll stretch for it; he will be hanged for it. Also telling a great lie: he stretched stoutly.
Twenty shillings. CANT.
Straw. CANT.
Hold your tongue. CANT.
See STALLING KEN. CANT.
The flower of fermenting wine, used by vintners to adulterate their wines.
Legs. To stir one's stumps; to walk fast.
The fifth and last of the most ancient order of canters, beggars that rather demand than ask CANT.

entries.word: SUCH A REASON PIST MY GOOSE, or MY GOOSE PIST
entries.text: Said when any one offers an absurd reason.
Strong liquor of any sort. To suck the monkey; see MONKEY. Sucky; drunk.
To pump. To draw from a man all be knows. The file sucked the noodle's brains: the deep one drew out of the fool all he knew.
A young chicken.
In the suds; in trouble, in a disagreeable situation, or involved in some difficulty.
Toasted bread soked in ale, sweetened with sugar, and grated nutmeg: it is eaten with cheese.
To have been in the sun; said of one that is drunk.
One who goes abroad on that day only, for fear of arrests.
A good fire in winter.
Prosperity.
Good liquor, of which there is not even a drop left sufficient to wet one's nail.
A landlady of an inn, or hostess.
One reeling drunk.
One standing in the pillory.
Hanged: persons who have been hanged are thus entered into the jailor's books.
One in a deadly suspence; a man just turned off at the gallows.
A camp publican: also one that pilfers gloves, tobacco boxes, and such small moveables.
The ace of hearts, knave of clubs, ace and duce of trumps, at whist: also the lubberly seamen, put to swab, and clean the ship.
A soldier. CANT.
To beat with a stick.
A shop. Any quantity of goods. As, plant the swag; conceal the goods. Rum swag; a shop full of rich goods. CANT.
To bully, brag, or boast, also to strut.
He keeps a swannery; i.e. all his geese are swans.
Easy to be imposed on, or taken in; also expert, dexterous clever. Sweet's your hand; said of one dexterous at stealing.

A disorder to which horses are extremely liable, particularly those of the subalterns of the army. This disorder is generally occasioned by remaining too long in one livery-stable or inn, and often arises to that height that it prevents their coming out at the stable door. The most certain cure is the unguentum aureum--not applied to the horse, but to the palm of the master of the inn or stable. N. B. Neither this disorder, nor its remedy, is mentioned by either Bracken, Bartlet, or any of the modern writers on farriery.
A hearty draught of liquor.
Thieves who travel the country under colour of buying old shoes, old clothes, &c. or selling brooms, mops, &c. CANT.
To drink greedily.
A drunkard, a sot.
A counterfeit old coin.
A ship. I shall have a swimmer; a cant phrase used by thieves to signify that they will be sent on board the tender.
To be hanged. He will swing for it; he will be hanged for it.
To beat stoutly.
Purser's swipes; small beer: so termed on board the king's ships, where it is furnished by the purser.
Drink, or any brisk or windy liquor. In North America, a mixture of spruce beer, rum, and sugar, was so called. The 17th regiment had a society called the Swizzle Club, at Ticonderoga, A. D. 1760.
To enlist in different regiments, and on receiving the bounty to desert immediately.
An exchange.
Sixpence.
A schoolmaster.
Silence, hold your tongue. TACE is Latin for a candle; a jocular admonition to be silent on any subject.
An expression meaning an assemblage of low people, the mobility of all sorts. To tag after one like a tantony pig: to follow one wherever one goes, just as St. Anthony is followed by his pig.
Imposed on, cheated.

Persons said to have been formerly hired to tell wonderful stories of giants and fairies, to lull their hearers to sleep. Talesman; the author of a story or report: I'll tell you my tale, and my talesman. Tale bearers; mischief makers, incendiaries in families.
A bottle, or two-quart pot.
To run tame about a house; to live familiarly in a family with which one is upon a visit. Tame army; the city trained bands.
A two-wheeled chaise, buggy, or noddy, drawn by two horses, one before the other: that is, AT LENGTH.
A room in Newgate, where debtors were confined, hence called Tangerines.
A sixpence. The kiddey tipped the rattling cove a tanner for luck; the lad gave the coachman sixpence for drink.
A sirreverence, human excrement.
Away they went tantwivy; away they went full speed. Tantwivy was the sound of the hunting horn in full cry, or that of a post horn.
Shoulder tappers: bailiffs.
Red tape; brandy. Blue or white tape; gin.
Thick and bad beer.
Don't lose a sheep for a halfpennyworth of tar: tar is used to mark sheep. A jack tar; a sailor.
A fib, or falsity.
A coarse cloth tarred over: also, figuratively, a sailor.
Sour, sharp, quick, pert.
Tit for tat; an equivalent.
False dice.
A watch. To flash a tatler: to wear a watch.
One that uses false dice.
A ragged fellow, whose clothes hang all in tatters.

A beat of the drum, of signal for soldiers to go to their quarters, and a direction to the sutlers to close the tap, and draw no more liquor for them; it is generally beat at nine in summer and eight in winter. The devil's tattoo; beating with one's foot against the ground, as done by persons in low spirits.
A schoolboy's game, played with small round balls made of stone dust, catted marbles. I'll be one upon your taw presently; a species of threat.
Beaten,
Thieves who snatch gentlemens swords from their sides. He drew the cull's tayle rumly; he snatched away the gentleman's sword cleverly.
An iron with which, when heated, press down the seams of clothes.
A chamber pot.
The drippings of liquor on a man's waistcoat.
An address to a supposed simple fellow, or nysey,
To-nap the teize; to receive a whipping. CANT.
Pumping a bailiff; a punishment formerly administered to any of that fraternity caught exercising their functions within the limits of Temple.
See BAYARD OF TEN TOES.
An usurer; more than five in the hundred being deemed usurious interest.
An estate in land.
A sixpence: from TESTON, a coin with a head on it.
He will not find out a way to set the Thames on fire; he will not make any wonderful discoveries, he is no conjuror.
A rogue, or man of bad character.
Intimate. They are as thick as two inkle-weavers.
You are a thief and a murderer, you have killed a baboon and stole his face; vulgar abuse.
Part of the wick or snuff, which falling on the tallow, burns and melts it, and causing it to gutter, thus steals it away.

Fellows who associate with all kinds of villains, in order to betray them, when they have committed any of those crimes which entitle the persons taking them to a handsome reward, called blood money. It is the business of these thief takers to furnish subjects for a handsome execution, at the end of every sessions.
A watch. The swell flashes a rum thimble; the gentleman sports a fine watch.
A custom practised at the universities, where two thirds of the original price is allowed by the upholsterers to the students for household goods returned to them within the year.
To be or sit upon thorns; to be uneasy, impatient, anxious for an event.
A person who goes in at one door of a church, and out at the other, without stopping.
A looseness, a violent purging.
Coughing and breaking wind backwards at the same time.
To go thorough stitch; to stick at nothing; over shoes, over boots.

The gallows, formerly consisting of three posts, over which were laid three transverse beams. This clumsy machine has lately given place to an elegant contrivance, called the NEW DROP, by which the use of that vulgar vehicle a cart, or mechanical instrument a ladder, is also avoided; the patients being left suspended by the dropping down of that part of the floor on which they stand. This invention was first made use of for a peer. See DROP.
Half common ale, mixed with stale and double beer.
Threepence.
To strangle.
The throat, or gullet.
To play on any instrument stringed with wire. A thrummer of wire; a player on the spinet, harpsichord, of guitar.
Threepence.
By rule of thumb: to do any thing by dint of practice. To kiss one's thumb instead of the book; a vulgar expedient to avoid perjury in taking a false oath.
Great! a thumping boy.
A great blow with a stick across the shoulders.
A young lass
A cat.
To run o'tick; take up goods upon trust, to run in debt. Tick; a watch. SEE SESSIONS PAPERS.
A licence.
Neat.
Sixpence; so called from its formerly being the fare for Crossing over from Gravesend to Tilbury Fort.
To tilt; to fight with a sword. To run full tilt against one; allusion to the ancient tilling with the lance.
A sword.
A light one--horse chaise without a head.
Little.
The best: perhaps from fruit, that growing at the top of the tree being generally the best, as partaking most of the sun. A tip-top workman; the best, or most excellent Workman.
Liquor.
Sots who are continually sipping.
Almost drunk.
An equivalent.
To suppress a laugh.

One reeling, and ready to fall at the least touch; also the childish amusement of riding upon the two ends of a plank, poised upon the prop underneath its centre, called also see-saw. Perhaps tatter is a rustic pronunciation of totter.
A gentle hand gallop, or canter.
Sixpence.
A sword.
The highway. High toby man; a highway-man. Low toby man; a footpad.
A plant, once in great estimation as a medicine: Tobacco hic Will make you well if you be sick. Tobacco hic If you be well will make you sick.
Originally the juice of the cocoa tree, and afterwards rum, water, sugar, and nutmeg.
To walk away. The cove was touting, but stagging the traps he toddled; be was looking out, and feeing the officers he walked away.
Beat all to a todge: said of anything beat to mash.
A coat. Cant.
The same. CANT.
Clothes. The swell is rum-togged. The gentleman is handsomely dressed.
A night man, one who empties necessary houses.
A simple fellow.
A tiresome story teller. It is coming by Tom Long, the carrier; said of any thing that has been long expected.
Soft Tommy, or white Tommy; bread is so called by sailors, to distinguish it from biscuit. Brown Tommy: ammunition bread for soldiers; or brown bread given to convicts at the hulks.
When two Sundays come together; never.
A silly fellow, or ninny. A mere tony: a simpleton.
The instrument of any person or faction, a cat's paw. See CATS PAW. TOOTH Music. Chewing.
A large stick. An ironical expression.
A violent blow on the head.
To sway away on all top ropes; to live riotously or extravagantly.

To cheat, or trick: also to insult: he thought to have topped upon me. Top; the signal among taylors for snuffing the candles: he who last pronounces that word word, is obliged to get up and perform the operation.--to be topped; to be hanged. The cove was topped for smashing queerscreens; he was hanged for uttering forged bank notes.
Drunk.

The eyes. Blast your top lights. See CURSE. Top SAIL. He paid his debts at Portsmouth with the topsail; i.e. he went to sea and left them unpaid. SCT soldiers are said to pay off their scores with the drum; that is, by marching away.
One that loves his bottle, a soaker. SEE TO SOAK.
One at the top or head of his profession.
The gallows. CANT.
The hangman. CANT.
A rich man.
The top side the other way; i.e. the wrong side upwards; some explain it, the top side turf ways, turf being always laid the wrong side upwards.
Bumfodder.
A drummer.
A fiddler.
A drunkard.
Giddy, hare-brained.
A look-out house, or eminence.

(From TUERI, to look about) Publicans fore-stalling guests, or meeting them on the road, and begging their custom; also thieves or smugglers looking out to see that the coast is clear. Touting ken; the bar of a public house.
A grenadier. The tow row club; a club or society of the grenadier officers of the line.
An oaken towel, a cudgel. To rub one down with an oaken towel; to beat or cudgel him.
Clipped money: they have been round the tower with it. CANT.
To overlook, to rise aloft as in a high tower.
A slap on the face, and a kick on the breech.
To go. Track up the dancers; go up stairs. CANT.

Broken mechanics, discharged footmen, and other low fellows, smuggled into the commission of the peace, who subsist by fomenting disputes, granting warrants, and otherwise retailing justice; to the honour of the present times, these nuisances are by no means, so common as formerly.
Thieves. Clever tradesmen; good thieves.
Sellers of old mended shoes and boots, between coblers and shoemakers.
To patch up vamp, or alter.
To come up with any body.
See CROCKER.
To understand trap; to know one's own interest.
Constables and thief-takers. CANT.
To inveigle, or ensnare.
To tip the traveller; to tell wonderful stories, to romance.
The square cap worn by the collegians. at the universities of Oxford and Cambridge.
A stout trencher man; one who has a good appetite, or, as the term is, plays a good knife and fork.
Threepence.
A prison: perhaps from tribulation.
A quirk or quibble in the law.
The point at which schoolboys stand to shoot their marbles at taw; also the spot whence bowlers deliver the bowl.
To play truant. To lay a man trigging; to knock him down.
State, dress. In a sad trim; dirty.--Also spruce or fine: a trim fellow.
Like master, like man.
Cheating, changing side, or beating. I'll trim his jacket; I'll thresh him. To be trimmed; to be shaved; I'll just step and get trimmed.
To hang; also Tyburn.
A whim, or maggot.
Hanging.
Toys, bawbles, or nicknacks.
To loiter or saunter about.
Coarse lace once much in fashion.
You will die the death of a trooper's horse, that is, with your shoes-on; a jocular method of telling any one he will be hanged.
Feet. To shake one's trotters at Bilby's ball, where the sheriff pays the fiddlers; perhaps the Bilboes ball, i.e. the ball of fetters: fetters and stocks were anciently called the bilboes.
To punish by course of law.
To exchange, swop, or barter; also a wheel such as ship's guns are placed upon.
To sound one's own trumpet; to praise one's self.
To be put to one's trumps: to be in difficulties, or put to one's shifts. Something may turn up trumps; something lucky may happen. All his cards are trumps: he is extremely fortunate.
Peas.

A nose. How fares your old trunk? does your nose still stand fast? an allusion to the proboscis or trunk of an elephant. To shove a trunk: to introduce one's self unasked into any place or company. Trunk-maker like; more noise than work.
A true friend.
To endeavour. To live by thieving. Coves who try it on; professed thieves.
See TRINING.
A it anniversary parasite, one who courts the acquaintance of nobility, whose caps are adorned with a gold tuft.

There were four t--ds for dinner: stir t--d, hold t--d, tread t--d, and mus-t--d: to wit, a hog's face, feet and chitterlings, with mustard. He will never sh--e a seaman's t--d; i.e. he will never make a good seaman.
On the turf; persons who keep running horses, or attend and bet at horse-races, are said to be on the turf.
A poulterer.
One who has changed his party from interested motives.
Acquitted; discharged.
A parson; because the clergy collect their tolls at our entrance into and exit from the world.
Perplexity, confusion, or any thing else: a fashionable term that for a while succeeded that of BORE. See BORE.
A north country name for a taylor.
In a great tweague: in a great passion. Tweaguey; peevish, passionate.
To pull: to tweak any one's nose.
A shilling.
Handsome; stilish. The cove is togged in twig; the fellow is dressed in the fashion.
To observe. Twig the cull, he is peery; observe the fellow, he is watching us. Also to disengage, snap asunder, or break off. To twig the darbies; to knock off the irons.
A mixture of half tea and half coffee; likewise brandy, beer, and eggs. A good twist; a good appetite. To twist it down apace; to eat heartily.
Executed, hanged.
To reproach a person, or remind him of favours conferred.
All in a twitter; in a fright. Twittering is also the note of some small birds, such as the robin, &c.
Two. CANT.
A man beating his hands against his sides to warm himself in cold weather; called also beating the booby, and cuffing Jonas.
A pawnbroker's: alluding to the three blue balls, the sign of that trade: or perhaps to its being two to one that the goods pledged are never redeemed.
A neckcloth.
A young thief or pickpocket, who in time will ripen into fruit borne by the deadly never-green.
A halter; see Latimer's sermon before. Edward VI. A. D. 1549.
A wig with the foretop combed over the eyes in a knowing style; such being much worn by the gentlemen pads, scamps, divers, and other knowing hands.
See TINEY.
Frolics, wild rambles.
One who boasts without reason, or, as the canters say, pisses more than he drinks.

To pawn any thing. I'll vamp it, and tip you the cole: I'll pawn it, and give you the money. Also to refit, new dress, or rub up old hats, shoes or other wearing apparel; likewise to put new feet to old boots. Applied more particularly to a quack bookseller.
Stockings.
To give one's vardy; i.e. verdict or opinion.
Now rogues and rascals, formerly yeoman's servants.
(Whip and Cambridge.) Natty, dashing. He is quite varment, he is quite the go. He sports a varment hat, coat, &c.; he is dressed like a gentleman Jehu.
Half a quarter of a sheet.
See BRAY.

entries.word: VICE ADMIRAL OF THE NARROW SEAS
entries.text: A drunken man that pisses under the table into his companions' shoes.
The stomach.

The art of cheating at cards, composed of the following associates: bankers, those who play booty; the gripe, he that betteth; and the person cheated, who is styled the vincent; the gains acquired, termage.
A name given to the person who with a whip in his hand, and a hat held before his eye, keeps the ring clear, at boxing-matches and cudgel-playing; also, in cant terms, a cloak.
An inferior in any office, or department.
A turnkey.
A parson, who at least once a week abuses his best benefactor, i.e. the devil.
A bribe.
A coach drawn by three horses.
A rude uncouth young fellow.
Undone, ruined, done up.
To be a match for one who attempts to cheat or deceive; to be on a footing, or in the secret. I'll be up with him; I will repay him in kind.
False dice that run high.
A great coat. CANT.
Figuratively used to signify the head. His upper story or garrets are unfurnished; i.e. he is an empty or foolish fellow.
[Called in some counties a leaping stock, in others a jossing block.] Steps for mounting a horse. He sits like a toad on a jossing block; said of one who sits ungracefully on horseback.
Testy, apt to take offence.

Go upright; a word used by shoemakers, taylors and their servants, when any money is given to make them drink, and signifies, Bring it all out in liquor, though the donor intended less, and expects change, or some of his money, to be returned. Three-penny upright. See THREEPENNY UPRIGHT,
Persons lately raised to honours and riches from mean stations.

Killed: a military saying, originating from a message sent by the late General Guise, on the expedition at Carthagena, where he desired the commander in chief to order him some more grenadiers, for those he had were all used up.
Footwabler; a contemptuous term for a foot soldier, frequently used by those of the cavalry.
An arch-frolicsome fellow.
Arch, gamesome, frolicsome.

Musicians of the lower order, who in most towns play under the windows of the chief inhabitants at midnight, a short time before Christmas, for which they collect a christmas-box from house to house. They are said to derive their name of waits from being always in waiting to celebrate weddings and other joyous events happening within their district.
An ensign of foot.
One who steals fowls, and hawks them from door to door.
A hawker of pamphlets, &c.

A mode of destroying devoted persons or officers in a mutiny or ship-board, by blindfolding them, and obliging them to walk on a plank laid over the ship's side; by this means, as the mutineers suppose, avoiding the penalty of murder.
To run up a score, which in alehouses is commonly recorded with chalk on the walls of the bar.
An exclamation used by thieves to inform their confederates that some police officers are at hand.
Rich, in good circumstances. To warm, or give a man a warming; to beat him. See CHAFED.
Paint for the face, or cosmetic water. Hog-wash; thick and bad beer.
Peevish, spiteful.
House of waste; a tavern or alehouse, where idle people waste both their time and money.
CHAIN, AND SEALS. A sheep's head And pluck.
A man who steals from ships or craft on the river.
His chops watered at it; he longed earnestly for it. To watch his waters; to keep a strict watch on any one's actions. In hot water: in trouble, engaged in disputes.
Very weak punch or beer.
One that robs ships in the river Thames.
Apt to shed tears.
A doctor who prescribes from inspecting the water of his patients. See PISS PROPHET.
Ears. CANT.
A one-horse chaise.
Silver plate, because melted by the receivers of stolen goods into wedges. CANT.
To take a part. The kiddey weeded the swell's screens; the youth took some of the gentleman's bank notes.
To come home by weeping cross; to repent.
To divide unfairly. To conceal part. A cant phrase used by thieves, where one of the party conceals some of the booty, instead of dividing it fairly amongst his confederates.
One who moistens his clay freely, in order to make it stick together.
A sharper. To cut a wheedle; to decoy by fawning or insinuation. Cant.
Regular drinking over the left thumb.
An impudent whelp; a saucy boy.

To follow a whereas; to become a bankrupt, to figure among princes and potentates: the notice given in the Gazette that a commission of bankruptcy is issued out against any trader, always beginning with the word whereas. He will soon march in the rear of a whereas.
A morning's draught, commonly white wine, supposed to whet or sharpen the appetite.
Words. Cant.

To tell or discover. He whiddles; he peaches. He whiddles the whole scrap; he discovers all he knows. The cull whiddled because they would not tip him a snack: the fellow peached because they would not give him a share, They whiddle beef, and we must brush; they cry out thieves, and we must make off. Cant.
An informer, or one that betrays the secrets of the gang.
Ancient name for fifers; also persons at the universities who examine candidates for degrees. A whiffling cur, a small yelping cur.
A low cry.
To complain.
A sword.

The tenth order of the canting crew, rogues who having learned a few sea terms, beg with counterfeit passes, pretending to be sailors shipwrecked on the neighbouring coast, and on their way to the port from whence they sailed.
To run away, to drink off greedily, to snatch. He whipped away from home, went to the alehouse, where he whipped off a full tankard, and coming back whipped off a fellow's hat from his head.
or pinch-gut vengeance, of which he that gets the most has the worst share. Weak or sour beer.
A sharp or subtle fellow.
A flimsy, frothy discourse or treatise, without solidity.
A great lie.
A shallow brown drinking bowl.
The throat. To wet one's whistle; to drink.
Rooms in the King's Bench and Fleet prison where drams are privately sold.

[i. e. Whittington's.] Newgate. Cant.--Five rum-padders are rubbed in the darkmans out of the whit, and are piked into the deuseaville; five highwaymen broke out of Newgate in the night, and are gone into the country.
Gin.
Cowardly, malicious.
A harmless lie, one not told with a malicious intent, a lie told to reconcile people at variance.
Geneva.
Geneva.
One who has taken the benefit of an act of insolvency, to defraud his creditors, is said to have been whitewashed.
Newgate; built or repaired by the famous lord mayor of that name.
Bad drink.
The four of clubs: from one James Wibling, who in the reign of King James I. grew rich by private gaming, and was commonly observed to have that card, and never to lose a game but when he had it not.
A casement; also a little door.
A man wearing a large wig.
Wigsby; a man wearing a wig.
Rogues trained up to stealing from their cradles.
A looseness.
A tedious uncertain pursuit, like the following a flock of wild geese, who are remarkably shy.
A penny,
To steal. The cull has won a couple of rum glimsticks; the fellow has stolen a pair of fine candlesticks.
A legacy, or any accidental accession of property.
Foolish projects.
A collector of the window tax.
Foolish. A windy fellow; a simple fellow.
To tip one the wink; to give a signal by winking the eye.
Plunder, goods, or money acquired by theft.
A taylor.
A blow, or reproach. I'll give you a wipe on the chops. That story gave him a fine wipe. Also a handkerchief.
A handkerchief. CANT.
To lengthen out or extend any book, letter, or discourse.
A foolish conceited fellow.
Gresham college.
Silver. Witcher bubber; a silver bowl. Witcher tilter; a silver-hilted sword. Witcher cully; a silversmith.
To boil. Pot wobbler; one who boils a pot.
A monstrous or canine appetite.

In a wood; bewildered, in a maze, in a peck of troubles, puzzled, or at a loss what course to take in any business. To look over the wood; to ascend the pulpit, to preach: I shall look over the wood at St. James's on Sunday next. To look through the wood; to stand in the pillory. Up to the arms in wood; in the pillory.
A bystander, who bets whilst another plays.
A taylor with a long bill.
A coffin. A man who dies in prison is said to go out with a wooden habeas. He went out with a wooden habeas; i.e. his coffin.
(Cambridge.) The last junior optime. See WRANGLER, OPTIME.
The pillory. See NORWAY NECKCLOTH.
A coilin.
A sheep. CANT.
Your wits are gone a woolgathering; saying to an absent man, one in a reverie, or absorbed in thought.
A soft-headed fellow.
Verbal critics, and also persons who use hard words in common discourse.
A punster, one who plays upon words.
To drink by word of mouth, i.e. out of the bowl or bottle instead, of a glass.
To worm out; to obtain the knowledge of a secret by craft, also to undermine or supplant. He is gone to the diet of worms; he is dead and buried, or gone to Rothisbone.

At CAMBRIDGE the first class (generally of twelve) at the annual examination for a degree. There are three classes of honours, wranglers, senior optimes, and junior optimes. Wranglers are said to be born with golden spoons in their mouths, the senior optimes with silver, and the junior with leaden ones. The last junior optime is called the wooden spoon. Those who are not qualified for honors are either in the GULF (that is, meritorious, but not deserving of being in the three first classes) or among the pollot [Proofreaders Note: Greek Letters] the many. See PLUCK, APOSTLES, &C.
A red cloak, called also a roquelaire.

entries.word: WRY MOUTH AND A PISSEN PAIR OF BREECHES
entries.text: Hanging.
Hanging day.
See WIN.
Eating. CANT.
To eat or stuff heartily.
A red herring: Yarmouth is a famous place for curing herrings.
A pye made of herrings highly spiced, which the city of Norwich is by charter bound to present annually to the king.
Milk. CANT.
Guineas.
To cry out. Yelper; a town cryer, also one apt to make great complaints on trifling occasions.
A contraction of yesterday.
A familiar expression of contempt for another's ignorance, as "ah! I see you're a young one." How d'ye do, young one?
To cry aloud, or howl.
The jester, jack pudding, or merry andrew, to a mountebank.
